item.title: PHP2Shell Attack Roots 25 Servers, Breaches U.S. Government-Affiliated Network
item.description:
A suspected Chinese 🇨🇳 state-aligned actor rooted 25 servers across four countries using a custom PHP2Shell exploit chain, breaching a U.S. 🇺🇸 government-affiliated Active Directory environment on October 23-24, 2026.
Key findings:
- The attack chain combines two vulnerability sets: PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS 9.2), unauthenticated RCE via PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on a firewall's appweb management server running PHP 8.0.30, chained with Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300, CVSS 7.8), a Linux kernel local privilege escalation. The exploit is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known PoC, developed specifically for the targeted firewall platform. This matters for detection: generic PHP2Shell signatures may not fire on it.
- The operation was highly automated and staged. The attacker used FOFA to fingerprint roughly 19,000 internet-exposed firewall management interfaces globally, ran a custom version scanner to reduce that to around 5,000 live systems, then filtered to ~240 targets in the U.S. 🇺🇸, Japan 🇯🇵, Taiwan 🇹🇼, and South Korea 🇰🇷 running the vulnerable PHP version. A batch runner then executed the full exploit chain, planted a PHP web shell in a publicly accessible directory, verified root, and logged results to a CSV. The entire target-selection and exploitation pipeline is consistent with AI-augmented development: nearly 40 recovered scripts share uniform code structure and commenting style, and the attacker's infrastructure contained Anthropic's Claude Code, API keys for FOFA, and an offensive platform called aiscan configured with DeepSeek and Kimi LLMs.
- Post-root activity on the three U.S. 🇺🇸 government-affiliated servers moved directly toward identity infrastructure. The attacker established a reverse SSH tunnel from the compromised perimeter firewall back to operator infrastructure at 11:35 a.m. UTC on October 24, 2026, then used that tunnel to reach an internal firewall management server not exposed to the internet. Active Directory targeting included LDAP service account password decryption, user enumeration, organization-themed password spraying across all accounts, and attempted creation of backdoor AD accounts. Whether any valid credentials were extracted or backdoor accounts survived is unconfirmed.
- Twenty-two of the 25 rooted servers outside the government environment remain parked with active web shells as of the report. The reverse SSH tunnel into the U.S. 🇺🇸 government network is assessed as likely still running. The attacker retains a fingerprinted list of ~19,000 targets they can return to as they develop offsets for additional OS builds. One government server crashed at 6:14 p.m. UTC on October 23 and never recovered, representing a potential availability impact alongside the confidentiality risk.
Practitioner takeaway: If your organization runs an internet-exposed firewall management interface, treat it as the initial access vector here and start with the perimeter. Hunt for PHP web shells in publicly accessible directories on the firewall OS, unexpected outbound SSH connections or reverse tunnels originating from the firewall process tree, and LDAP enumeration or password-spray activity against Active Directory that correlates in time with any firewall anomaly. On the AD side, look for newly created accounts, LDAP service account authentication events, and spray patterns using organization-themed passwords. The report itself does not publish an IOC list or detection rules.

item.title: AL26-028: Ongoing Help Desk Voice Phishing Campaign Targeting Canadian Organizations
item.description:
Canadian 🇨🇦 organizations in legal and financial sectors face an active vishing campaign tied to UNC6671/BlackFile, bypassing MFA via real-time adversary-in-the-middle relay and rotating lure domains.
Key findings:
- The threat actor, publicly linked to UNC6671 and the BlackFile operation, impersonates internal IT or help desk staff over phone calls, Microsoft Teams, and spoofed help desk numbers. Callers invent urgent pretexts: passkey migrations, MFA enrolments, or forced password resets. They reference internal IT staff names and fake deadlines to build credibility, and drop the call if the employee tries to verify independently. The Canadian 🇨🇦 Centre for Cyber Security has tracked related infrastructure naming Canadian 🇨🇦 organizations since January 2026, with October activity concentrated on the legal sector.
- Employees are directed to organisation-branded adversary-in-the-middle pages hosted on generic root domains. The alert gives example patterns: the targeted organization's name appearing as a subdomain of onetimesso[.]com or registermymfa[.]com, or baked directly into newly registered domains following patterns like org-namesso[.]com or org-nameinternal[.]com. Domain naming mixes action words (activate, enroll, register, deploy, set) with authentication terms (passkey, sso, mfa, 2fa, okta). The page relays credentials and MFA tokens to the legitimate identity provider in real time, handing the actor a fully authenticated session and defeating conventional TOTP-based MFA.
- Post-compromise activity is systematic and fast. The actor registers attacker-controlled MFA methods or devices, deletes password-reset and security notification emails, and resets passwords for non-SSO applications. Automated scripts and Microsoft Graph are used to access and exfiltrate data from Microsoft 365, SharePoint, and OneDrive. Extortion demands follow data theft, confirming the financially motivated profile.
- The forensic footprint centers on identity provider and Microsoft 365 audit logs. Responders should look for new MFA method or device registrations outside normal business hours, high-volume or scripted file access in SharePoint and OneDrive, deletion of security notification emails from mailboxes, and sign-ins originating from commercial VPNs, hosting providers, or residential proxies. Newly registered domains incorporating the organization's name are an early-warning signal worth monitoring continuously.
Takeaway: If you are investigating a suspected compromise, revoke all active sessions and tokens immediately, remove unauthorized MFA registrations, reset credentials, and preserve identity provider and Microsoft 365 audit logs before touching anything else: that log data is your timeline. Hunt for Microsoft Graph API access spikes, bulk file reads on SharePoint or OneDrive, and security-email deletions as indicators of the post-access exfiltration phase. The report does not publish a discrete IOC list, but the domain-pattern guidance is actionable for proactive monitoring and threat hunting against newly registered domains matching your organization's name combined with the authentication-related terms described above.

item.title: Volt Typhoon Used Covert Silent Train Network in Four Zero-Day Exploitation Campaigns
item.description:
Volt Typhoon's Silent Train network linked to four zero-day campaigns against US 🇺🇸 critical infrastructure, telecom, defense, and control-plane technologies, with hundreds of victims identified across sectors including energy, water, aviation, and rail.
Key findings:
- Four confirmed zero-day campaigns run through Silent Train: CVE-2024-39717 (Versa Director file upload, previously known), CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 (N-able N-central insecure deserialization and command injection), CVE-2026-20127 (Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller authentication bypass), and CVE-2026-16812 (Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator OS command injection). A suspected zero-day in Quest KACE, patched October 2025, is also attributed to the group and estimated to have hit more than 30 victims. The repeated focus on endpoint management platforms, SD-WAN orchestrators, and network control-plane systems is deliberate: compromise one and you inherit downstream visibility across an entire enterprise.
- Silent Train is a layered multi-hop relay framework, not a traditional botnet. Sessions originate from VPS infrastructure outside the US 🇺🇸, route through compromised non-US SOHO and IoT devices for origin concealment, then exit through US-based compromised devices to defeat geofencing and IP reputation controls. Average session length was roughly four hours, with some lasting only minutes. Post-session cleanup removed SSH keys, temporary services, configuration files, and every living-off-the-land utility deployed during the operation, leaving minimal on-disk artifacts for responders to recover.
- 27 device classes have been enrolled as relay nodes, spanning TP-Link, Intelbras, Ruckus Wireless, SATO, NETGEAR, Zyxel, Cambium, Fortinet, Cisco, PRTG, Mirth Connect, and CyberPanel. Compartmentalization is deliberate and structural: Intelbras modems appear exclusively as relay nodes, while Netgear Orbi and Fortinet FortiGate appliances serve as US-based exit points. By early 2025 the architecture matured into a hybrid model retaining enterprise-grade devices for one to three months, and introduced reverse-tunnel variants using open-source proxies Chisel and FRP to push traffic upstream.
- Silent Train activity surged immediately after the January 2024 disruption of KV-botnet, with Volt Typhoon rebuilding into an ephemeral, geographically distributed model as a direct operational response to law-enforcement pressure. Hawaii, California, and Texas dominate the US 🇺🇸 victimology, reflecting the concentration of military installations, satellite communications, defense contractors, and critical logistics in those states. Victimology across all sectors points to pre-positioning for access that would matter most during a crisis in the Indo-Pacific.
Takeaway: The near-complete post-operation cleanup makes log and memory forensics the highest-yield recovery path. Hunt for transient SSH service creation and removal events on SOHO and enterprise edge devices, unexpected Chisel or FRP process execution, and short-lived SSH authorized_keys entries that no longer exist at collection time. On management platforms (SD-WAN controllers, RMM systems, network orchestrators), prioritize authentication logs around the CVE IDs above for unusual auth patterns preceding any config or credential access. IOCs and additional technical detail are in the Black Lotus Labs report.

item.title: LevelBlue TTP Briefing Q3 2026: Trusted Access Fuels Data Theft
item.description:
LevelBlue SpiderLabs Q3 2026 IR data: exfiltration now outpaces encryption as the primary attacker goal, MFA bypassed in 79% of BEC cases, and dwell time keeps shrinking as attackers accelerate with AI-assisted tooling.
Key findings:
- Exfiltration overtook file viewing/access as the most common data-at-risk outcome for the first time, appearing in 83% of intrusion cases vs. 67% for encryption. Exfiltration-only attacks were the fastest-growing incident category, with rclone, MegaSync, WinSCP, 7-Zip, and WinRAR consistently observed in attacker workflows for staging and transfer. BEC led all incident types at 32%, followed by network intrusions without ransomware at 22%, and ransomware at 20%. Detection built around encryption events is now missing a growing share of intrusions: the signal to build on is large outbound transfers, unusual archive creation, and new cloud storage destinations.
- CVE-2026-72898, a CVSS 10 unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in Metabase, was actively exploited in Q3 incidents and delivered a fully self-contained intrusion path. LevelBlue SpiderLabs observed threat actors creating new admin accounts post-exploitation, abusing Metabase's connected AI engines to pivot to third-party systems, and exfiltrating and extorting victims from there. Also actively exploited this quarter: CVE-2024-40762, CVE-2024-40766, and CVE-2024-53704 in SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN, CVE-2024-53705 (SonicWall SSRF), CVE-2026-0257 in PAN-OS GlobalProtect, CVE-2025-13407 in the Gravity Forms WordPress plugin, and CVE-2022-26923 in Active Directory Domain Services. External remote services (RDP, VPN) and exploited vulnerabilities each tied for second place as initial access vectors at 14%, together accounting for more than a quarter of all initial access behind phishing at 42%.
- MFA bypass occurred in 79% of BEC incidents where MFA was enabled. The dominant technique shifted away from token interception toward vishing and help-desk impersonation that convinces victims to enroll an attacker-controlled device, making the access appear legitimate from the inside. The report also notes increased abuse of machine identity and token-based access that sidesteps MFA prompts entirely, which partially accounts for the bypass stat. API key exposure drove a spike in Technology and Software sector targeting, with threat actors using AI tooling to hunt for exposed, long-lived, over-permissioned keys as a direct path into custom applications and their downstream customers.
- Persistence was most commonly maintained via remote access tools including ScreenConnect and MeshAgent. Credential theft relied heavily on Mimikatz and DCSync. Average dwell time continued to compress, with 56% of incidents resolved in 0 to 10 days, and the report attributes this partly to attackers using AI tools to execute intrusions in hours rather than days.
Practitioner takeaway: Prioritize hunting on outbound data movement, not just encryption events. Monitor cloud storage destinations and archive utility execution (rclone, MegaSync, 7-Zip, WinRAR, WinSCP). For identity, add device enrollment monitoring alongside MFA, implement short token lifetimes, and build conditional-access policies that flag anomalous token use. Patch internet-facing applications holding sensitive data, not just network appliances: CVE-2026-72898 in Metabase is a CVSS 10 with confirmed exploitation this quarter. The full CVE list and intrusion-path TTP data are in the report.

item.title: Cache Me If You Can: XSS in Cloudflare's /cdn-cgi/image/
item.description:
A three-part chain delivers same-origin XSS through Cloudflare's /cdn-cgi/image/ endpoint, bypassing svg-hush sanitization and CSP via a Chromium cache behavior that has been largely overlooked outside CTF circles.
Key findings:
- The svg-hush sanitizer (written in Rust) escapes ordinary XML attribute values but not namespace URI values. The xml-rs serialization layer writes xmlns: prefix URIs directly to output without escaping, so a crafted SVG with a payload inside an xmlns attribute value survives sanitization and lands executable in the response body. The root element uses a legitimate SVG namespace prefix to pass the sanitizer's namespace check, while the injected default namespace carries the break-out string.
- /cdn-cgi/image/ forwards Cache-Control and X-* response headers from the origin image to the client. RFC 7234 defines a qualified no-cache directive, Cache-Control: no-cache="field-name", that tells a cache to strip the named header when serving a stored response. Chromium implements this selective-header stripping in HttpResponseHeaders::AddNonCacheableHeaders. Firefox and Safari do not. Sending Cache-Control: no-cache="Content-Security-Policy" from the origin image causes Chromium to cache the response body but drop the CSP header. A subsequent history-back navigation via a window.opener relationship (ineligible for BFCache) forces Chromium to reload from HTTP disk cache, serving the body with no CSP present. This technique was demonstrated in the SECCON 2022 spanote CTF write-up but had not previously been applied to production CDN infrastructure at this scale.
- For zones using the default "This zone only" image source restriction, the researchers needed an open redirect reachable from an allowed origin. They found that when Cloudflare Access is enabled on any hostname in a zone, /cdn-cgi/access/logout?returnTo= is available on every proxied hostname and will redirect to cloudflare[.]com subdomains. A redirect endpoint at discord-mock-oauth.research.cloudflare[.]com/authorize?redirect_uri= completed the chain. The image fetcher follows redirects without re-validating the destination against the source configuration, so the chain reached an attacker-controlled SVG.
- The Cache-Control primitive extends beyond Cloudflare. On Netlify Image CDN, supplying Cache-Control: no-cache="Content-Security-Policy, Content-Type" strips both headers from the cached response. Without Content-Type, Chromium MIME-sniffs the body. An SVG/HTML polyglot using a processing instruction (<?a ><script>... a?>) stays inert during XML-mode sanitization (SVGO's removeScripts only registers an element visitor, not a PI visitor) and becomes active HTML when the cached response is sniffed as text/html. On S3-backed origins, AWS presigned URL parameters response-content-type and response-cache-control provide direct header override, extending the attack to any custom domain, CNAME, or reverse proxy that preserves query parameters, including Google Cloud Storage V4 signed URLs via response-content-type.
Takeaway: Any proxy, image optimizer, or object-storage layer that forwards or permits override of Cache-Control is part of your CSP security boundary, not just the application layer. When reviewing image-optimization or CDN configurations, verify that origin servers cannot inject Cache-Control: no-cache="Content-Security-Policy" or no-cache="Content-Type" into responses. In Chromium-targeted threat scenarios, treat history-back navigations from window.opener contexts as a potential CSP-strip trigger and check whether your Content-Security-Policy is present on cache-revalidation responses. The full technical write-up including proof-of-concept code is in the report.

An SVG/HTML polyglot using a processing instruction (<?a ><script>... a?>) stays inert during XML-mode sanitization (SVGO's removeScripts only registers an element visitor, not a PI visitor) and becomes active HTML when the cached response is sniffed as text/html. On S3-backed origins, AWS presigned URL parameters response-content-type and response-cache-control provide direct header override, extending the attack to any custom domain, CNAME, or reverse proxy that preserves query parameters, including Google Cloud Storage V4 signed URLs via response-content-type.

Takeaway: Any proxy, image optimizer, or object-storage layer that forwards or permits override of Cache-Control is part of your CSP security boundary, not just the application layer. When reviewing image-optimization or CDN configurations, verify that origin servers cannot inject Cache-Control: no-cache="Content-Security-Policy" or no-cache="Content-Type" into responses. In Chromium-targeted threat scenarios, treat history-back navigations from window.opener contexts as a potential CSP-strip trigger and check whether your Content-Security-Policy is present on cache-revalidation responses. The full technical write-up including proof-of-concept code is in the report.

item.title: Managed for Malice: How Attackers Turn MDM into Remote Access
item.description:
Attackers are weaponizing legitimate MDM platforms from Hexnode and Rippling as a persistent, privileged deployment channel, using social engineering to enroll victim devices before dropping unauthorized ScreenConnect instances that survive initial removal.
Key findings:
- The Hexnode case began with phishing emails using business-themed lures like "ATTN: Official Invitation to Submit Proposal." A link downloaded eD0cuSign_Installer.msi from hxxps://webdocusign.viewportal[.]es/Windows/download/index.php, a file designed to mimic a DocuSign installer that instead silently installed Hexnode Gateway, the Hexnode agent, and PostgreSQL components. ScreenConnect then connected to attacker-controlled relay.bobdthjau[.]com:8041. When the RMM was removed, the MDM remained, and the actor simply redeployed ScreenConnect hours later to the same relay, triggering a second alert.
- The Rippling case shows enrollment does not require a user running an MSI. A receptionist clicked a fake Microsoft Teams calendar link at teams-microsoftcom5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592.kiratham[.]com, which redirected through an enroll14.php endpoint. Within roughly one minute, a Rippling enrollment registry key appeared on the system. The agent installed as C:\Rippling\daemon.exe with SYSTEM-level permissions, and approximately 35 minutes later ScreenConnect was staged and executed as SYSTEM, connecting to relay.pronconetydesire[.]online:8041.
- The critical forensic insight here is persistence through trusted management infrastructure, not malware. Removing the RMM without removing the MDM enrollment leaves the attacker holding a privileged, legitimate deployment channel. The MDM is the persistence mechanism; the RMM is just the payload delivered through it. Incident response that stops at the RMM is incomplete.
- Detection opportunity: the attack chain produces a sequenced, correlatable signal across telemetry sources. Watch for the appearance of MDM enrollment registry keys following a user web browsing session, the download of an MDM agent MSI to an unusual path such as C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\mdm\, and ScreenConnect or other RMM processes spawning with SYSTEM as their parent context shortly after. Outbound connections to unfamiliar relay domains on port 8041 are a notable network artifact in both cases.
- Neither Hexnode nor Rippling carries any fault here. The report is explicit: no vulnerability in either platform was exploited. Reputation-based trust in software is insufficient when the software is legitimately operating under attacker-controlled enrollment. This is the same abuse pattern seen with rogue RMM deployments, now one layer deeper in the management stack.
Hunt for unexpected MDM enrollment events by reviewing registry keys associated with known MDM agents and looking for MDM agent binaries installed outside of an authorized change window. IOCs including the delivery URL, both attacker-controlled ScreenConnect relay domains, and the lookalike Teams enrollment URLs are listed in the report.

item.title: Byte Debt: From an HTTP Header Typo to Cross-User Session Fixation
item.description:
CVE-2026-102479 in Eclipse Vert.x HTTP/1.x decoder lets a single misspelled header desync request boundaries, enabling silent request erasure, DoS, and cross-user session fixation against shared reverse proxy connections.
Key findings:
- The root cause lives in VertxHttpRequestDecoder's length-based header optimization. For 14-byte headers, the decoder checks prefix and suffix only, never byte offset 8. This means Content-Xength is silently treated as a valid Content-Length, while every tested front-end proxy (Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik, Caddy, Apache httpd, nghttpx) ignores it as an unknown custom header. No conflicting Transfer-Encoding needed, just one misspelled header is enough to split request framing between the two layers.
- The attack chain progresses in three stages. First, a Content-Xength header with no body causes Vert.x to wait for bytes the proxy never sends, hanging threads for DoS. Second, the "double-desync" technique borrows from published HTTP/1.1 desync research: request A opens the byte debt, request B carries hidden spliced requests C and D inside its body, and the backend serves C's response to the attacker while D sits orphaned in the socket. Third, the dangling byte technique is the breakthrough: D is left one byte short of its declared body, so no response fires immediately, the proxy's socket check sees a clean buffer, returns the connection to the pool, and the next real visitor's first byte satisfies D's debt, causing the backend to fire D's response at them.
- The practical impact demonstrated end to end is cross-user session fixation. Request D is crafted as a POST /login using attacker-controlled credentials. An unsuspecting visitor with no cookies receives the resulting 303 redirect setting a session cookie for the attacker's account, dropping them silently into that account's data. Against a 16-connection pool, roughly 25 to 35 percent of subsequent traffic is poisoned. The same primitive enables injecting reflected XSS payloads into innocent users browsing normally, and forced redirects to attacker-controlled phishing pages via any redirect parameter, all without requiring the victim to click anything.
- Affected versions are vertx-core 5.0.0 through 5.0.12, 5.1.0 through 5.1.9, and 5.2.0 only. The fix lands in 5.1.10 and 5.2.1 via a canonicalization correction in the header parser. The JFrog report confirmed PoCs against strimzi/strimzi-kafka-bridge (0.33.0), apache/camel-quarkus, and TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks when deployed behind a front-end proxy. vertx-core carries over 300 million cumulative Maven downloads, but the exposure window is limited to those three modern 5.x release bands.
- Detection opportunity is narrow at the network layer because the malicious header looks like an ordinary custom header to any proxy log. The evidence to hunt is behavioral: look for backend connections that close without completing a response cycle, unexpected 303 redirects setting session cookies on requests that carried none, and any log entries where a login endpoint responds to a request that originated from a connection the proxy had marked idle. Application-layer logs showing session cookies assigned to accounts that did not authenticate in that same request cycle are the strongest indicator of exploitation in progress.
Patch to io.vertx:vertx-core 5.1.10 or 5.2.1 immediately if you deployed any 5.x release before those versions behind a reverse proxy. If you cannot patch now, audit backend connection pool logs for hung connections and review session creation events for cookies issued without a corresponding authentication event in the same connection context.

item.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0: From Startup Hooks to Credential Theft
item.description:
Trojanized LiteLLM 1.107.0 pushed to PyPI and Docker on Oct 21 hooks Python's startup routine to steal credentials before any app code runs. Supply chain attack traced to a months-old unrotated key that handed attackers full CI/CD control.
Key findings:
- The attack chain began May 27 when an opencode.json file containing a master key was committed to a public repo, overwritten but never rotated. By October 10 the attacker used that key to query the Agent Platform API, retrieved a GitHub CLI OAuth token for a BerriAI org owner (bypassing 2FA), then on October 21 stood up a typosquatted repo named Berri-AI/litellm and hijacked the official release pipeline. A second compromised maintainer account was used to approve the production deployment. The attacker maintained access for 11 days before deploying the payload.
- The malicious files cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py land in the root site-packages directory, not the litellm/ package folder. cook.pth fires a single-line "import cook" at interpreter startup, cook[.]py Base64/zlib-decodes an embedded payload (internally labeled PRIVCOLLECT) and runs it in a daemon thread, and sitecustomize[.]py runs a polling loop that fetches a live C2 address from raw.githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain[.]txt then compiles and executes whatever code the /codepy endpoint returns, all in memory with no signature check. TTPs: T1195.001, T1574, T1059.006, T1102.001.
- The credential harvester targets AI coding assistant configs, IDE auth files, source control and package manager credentials, .env files, cloud CLI credential caches, container service-account files, procfs process environments on Linux, browser credential stores and history (Chromium and Firefox, T1555.003), SSH and GPG key material, CI/CD and Vault configs, and LiteLLM proxy database tables via an ORM child process (500-row limit per table). Collected data is AES-256-CBC encrypted with a fresh 32-byte key per run, the session key is wrapped with a hardcoded 4096-bit RSA public key, then exfiltrated via HTTP POST to hxxp://www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck with header X-Token: XWiA8gZNa7NcX2XRoAEb and the payload hash in X-SHA256 (T1041, T1560.002). A sentinel file at /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb marks successful exfiltration; /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock prevents duplicate RAT instances.
- Confirmed SHA-256 hashes for the poisoned wheels: macOS x86-64 sha256:7598727f209d717041db37f7dca271d3a7d328a279890e0e1d55375729aeb86d, macOS ARM64 sha256:0aaf7ba346d41ef2f40390436738b001180d5a1c03aa093f121078a9969d9a1a, Linux manylinux x86-64 sha256:462d0c9f67ca522d9e0e4acd245e90b36ce0d5353604a66bb7c43a1ec4a6fcf7, Linux manylinux ARM64 sha256:668169d35b87bf51324080390b1b1c5ab12bd335cfe5f1a99e3689abd5e02ae6, Linux musllinux x86-64 sha256:1bbce8caa94f01c0aaa0b7ddae51553a8a32e1ce53d96d44fe583272aff7ad00, Linux musllinux ARM64 sha256:c2e32d0ce2548aa662c18bf5001911a79fe5b30cf8357132275add02fdcde054, Windows x86-64 sha256:12d4ccc5c6f8d35cf4f2cf233b7f3e418e863e657d81ff5f5fc9e210005b9484. Docker image index sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not invoke Python or pip inside a suspect environment to check for the package; that alone triggers the payload. Hunt site-packages for cook.pth, cook[.]py, and sitecustomize[.]py, and check /tmp for .pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb and remote_code_loader.lock. Watch egress for POST traffic to litellm[.]dev and DNS queries resolving through raw.githubusercontent[.]com to the letters9813 path. Remediation requires full environment rebuild, not uninstall. Treat every secret accessible to the affected process as compromised and rotate immediately. IOCs, hashes, and ATT&CK mappings are in the ThreatMon report.

item.title: The Doorway Botnet: Inside a Large-Scale IoT and Network Device Compromise Campaign
item.description:
The Doorway botnet has systematically compromised routers, cameras, and enterprise servers globally, with 11,363 device joins recorded in a single hour and 41 GB of operational data left exposed by the operators themselves.
Key findings:
- CloudSEK's investigation began with 41 GB of exposed operational data left accessible by the Doorway operators, revealing the inner workings of the campaign at an unusual level of detail. The data contained 59 exploit modules targeting IoT devices, network gear, and enterprise servers, alongside automated credential stuffing logic designed to move through device populations at scale.
- The attack chain combines known vulnerability exploitation with brute-force credential attacks. Devices compromised include consumer and enterprise routers, surveillance cameras, and servers, all folded into proxy infrastructure rather than used for traditional DDoS or spam purposes. The botnet's primary value appears to be as a commercial proxy network, routing third-party traffic through victim devices.
- The 11,363 device joins in a single hour is the sharpest indicator of the campaign's operational tempo. At that rate, device turnover and fresh compromise happen continuously, meaning the active device count understates total victim exposure across the campaign's lifetime.
- The 59 exploit modules represent a broad targeting surface. Rather than focusing on a single vendor or CVE, the Doorway operation maintains a module library that can be aimed at whichever device population presents the weakest resistance, a characteristic of mature, commercially motivated botnet operations rather than a targeted threat actor.
Practitioners responding to suspected proxy abuse or unexplained outbound traffic on IoT or network devices should pull authentication logs for rapid sequential failed logins followed by a success, check for new or modified scheduled tasks, cron jobs, and startup scripts, and look for outbound connections to unfamiliar IPs on non-standard ports that persist across reboots. The CloudSEK report contains the IOC details from the exposed operational data.

item.title: CA-26-043: Aokigahara Infostealer Marks Shift in Commodity Malware with Dedicated AI Harvesting
item.description:
Aokigahara infostealer adds purpose-built collection routines targeting local AI coding assistants, marking a commodity malware shift that turns developer workstations into cloud and pipeline pivot points.
Key findings:
- Aokigahara (also tracked as Aoki, with possible lineage to Kamidere or Stygian) is a modular Windows infostealer first documented in 2026. Newer samples confirmed by independent analysis to have added AI-specific collection that earlier versions lacked, making this a family-level capability expansion, not just a configuration tweak. No operator or intrusion set attribution has been established.
- The dedicated routines harvest authentication files, session tokens, and local application databases from a broad product list: Claude Code and Desktop, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, JetBrains AI Assistant, Amazon Q, Kiro, and Codeium. Because most of these tools store session state in predictable, unencrypted directories, collection requires no exploit, only standard user-level execution. MITRE ATT&CK T1552.001 (Credentials In Files) covers this path, alongside T1555 for browser and password-manager data.
- Exfiltration uses AES-GCM encryption over an X25519 key exchange, uploading data in labeled chunks via HTTP POST to /gate/handshake, /gate/chunk, and /gate/complete endpoints. The Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 user agent combined with Aokigahara X-* headers is a network-layer signal, though the report cautions against relying on User-Agent alone. Exfiltration maps to T1041. Delivery vector remains unconfirmed; developer-focused campaigns commonly abuse malicious search ads, trojanized npm or PyPI packages, and rogue ISO or MSI files.
- The strategic impact is cross-boundary exposure. A single compromised developer workstation with harvested AI-tool tokens, Git credentials, SSH keys, and cloud configs (.aws, .ssh, .git-credentials) can give an adversary indirect access to private source repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and cloud production environments without ever touching those systems directly.
Hunt lead: search EDR file events for any process reading .claude, .codex, .gemini, .copilot, Cursor or Windsurf state.vscdb, Amazon Q or Kiro data, .aws, .ssh, and .git-credentials within a short interval. Cross that endpoint match immediately against AI provider, Git, cloud, and CI/CD audit logs for token use from new source IPs, new devices, or unusual automation. On the network side, flag the /gate/handshake, /gate/chunk, /gate/complete POST sequence. If compromise is suspected, isolate the host, revoke all exposed tokens from a clean system, and review audit logs from the earliest suspected compromise window before rebuilding. IOCs and technical artifacts are available in the Deepwatch Guardian Platform.

The Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 user agent combined with Aokigahara X-* headers is a network-layer signal, though the report cautions against relying on User-Agent alone. Exfiltration maps to T1041. Delivery vector remains unconfirmed; developer-focused campaigns commonly abuse malicious search ads, trojanized npm or PyPI packages, and rogue ISO or MSI files.

- The strategic impact is cross-boundary exposure. A single compromised developer workstation with harvested AI-tool tokens, Git credentials, SSH keys, and cloud configs (.aws, .ssh, .git-credentials) can give an adversary indirect access to private source repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and cloud production environments without ever touching those systems directly.

Hunt lead: search EDR file events for any process reading .claude, .codex, .gemini, .copilot, Cursor or Windsurf state.vscdb, Amazon Q or Kiro data, .aws, .ssh, and .git-credentials within a short interval. Cross that endpoint match immediately against AI provider, Git, cloud, and CI/CD audit logs for token use from new source IPs, new devices, or unusual automation. On the network side, flag the /gate/handshake, /gate/chunk, /gate/complete POST sequence. If compromise is suspected, isolate the host, revoke all exposed tokens from a clean system, and review audit logs from the earliest suspected compromise window before rebuilding. IOCs and technical artifacts are available in the Deepwatch Guardian Platform.

item.title: Camera Management Software Compromise Leads to Malware Deployment
item.description:
Camera management software (CMS.exe) abused as initial access in multiple incidents, leading to DLL sideloading via a legitimate Microsoft binary and C2 beaconing to 144.172.116[.]37.
Key findings:
- Initial access came through a compromised camera management platform, CMS.exe, installed at C:\Program Files (x86)\CMS\. Huntress could not fully attribute the software vendor, but notable strings inside the binary, including "developerslavery", "d3e3v4e3l9o9p0e3r4s2l9a1v4e3r4y6", and a reference to hxxp://cloudapi.3r-dataware[.]com/sso/, link it to a Korean company called 3R Global. The kvision[.]ai website hosts a CMS package containing those same strings, presented as a possible but not definitive source.
- Post-compromise, the attacker dropped rs.win32.exe (SHA256: 1fb4af4862643dcab1459872f723f574f1a588855b020916b600df5c20681144) into C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\CMS\RemoteSetup\, a user-writable path outside the protected application directory. It was launched with a command line supplying a remote IP, port 8000, hardcoded credential "admin" / "1234567a7654321", and file references, behavior consistent with a reverse shell establishing attacker-controlled remote access.
- The legitimate Microsoft Windows Parental Control Monitor binary, WpcMon.exe, was then dropped into C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WpcMon\, far from its expected home in C:\Windows\system32. Placing it in AppData was intentional: the attacker staged two modified DLLs, samcli.dll (SHA256: 8f8e88c54a9c56174974711eff99b4beb79536642fcca1902acdc3d4b1fd1035) and IPHLPAPI.DLL (SHA256: 70b2345302264c41504d59e6a63d6d908969740424b42b7373f10b4c8d74c87a), alongside it. Both masquerade as zlib compression libraries but carry beaconing functionality, contacting C2 at 144.172.116[.]37 via DLL sideloading when WpcMon.exe runs.
- Persistence was achieved by writing a reference to WpcMon.exe under the user's Run registry key, so the beacon relaunches on every sign-in. The process tree shows WpcMon.exe spawning from rs.win32.exe, which in turn traces back to CMS.exe: a clear forensic chain connecting initial access through the reverse shell to the sideloaded payload.
- The attacker's approach deliberately exploits a low-scrutiny software category. Camera management tools rarely appear in threat models, may lack application logging, and are often installed in user-accessible paths. Here, the absence of CMS application logs directly limited visibility into how the software itself was compromised, a gap defenders should factor into their coverage model.
Takeaway: Hunt for the full chain the report describes. Look for WpcMon.exe running outside C:\Windows\system32, specifically from AppData paths. Check the user Run key for unexpected WpcMon.exe entries. Review process ancestry for CMS.exe spawning rs.win32.exe or WpcMon.exe. Look for outbound connections to 144.172.116[.]37. Apply application control to block unapproved executables and DLLs in user-writable paths. IOCs are in the report.

item.title: False Protection, Emptied Accounts: The Seven Android Trojan Families Targeting Indian Banking Apps
item.description:
CyberDakait, a financially-motivated Android threat cluster, has hit Indian 🇮🇳 banking customers with 7 distinct trojan families since July 2025, compromising nearly 18,000 devices and intercepting 7.6 million SMS messages.
Key findings:
- The attack chain opens with smishing and vishing calls impersonating representatives from 11 Indian 🇮🇳 banks and 2 government programs, pitching a fake "Credit Card Protection Plan" deactivation. A WhatsApp link drops victims onto a phishing page where any button click silently downloads an APK hosted on GitHub, lending the payload apparent legitimacy. The dropper then fakes a Google Play update screen while covertly installing the main RAT and an XMRig-based cryptomining module (d-miner), and prompts the victim to disable battery optimization to keep the malware running persistently.
- All 7 families (cyb3rx, appkjl, godz, d-passive, d-shine, GhostBat/GhostGrab, tenxen) share core RAT capabilities: SMS interception and exfiltration, SMS forwarding and sending, phone call forwarding, and credit card credential harvesting via overlay attacks. Despite identical campaign objectives and phishing infrastructure, each family uses distinct C2 channels (Telegram bots, Firebase, or remote HTTP backends), unique database schemas, and independent command sets, confirming separate development. C2 commands across families include call_forward_activate, callForward, smsForward, KeyLogger, custom_ussd, and enableCallForwarding.
- Group-IB identified 2,364 unique victim devices via device UUIDs in Telegram bot "new app installation" check-in messages, and an additional 15,596 via exposed Firebase infrastructure, totaling 17,960 confirmed compromised devices. From those devices, 7,611,443 SMS messages were exfiltrated, including OTPs, transaction alerts, card numbers, CVV codes, PAN card details, and Aadhaar numbers, forwarded in near real time to attacker-controlled Telegram bots and Firebase nodes.
- GhostBat's development environment was partially exposed: Telegram screenshots from 2024 confirm the actors compiled payloads directly on Android devices using AIDE, MT Manager, Apktool M, and Acode, storing .java files and AndroidIDEProjects folders on-device. Separately, a GitHub repository (ranidevisingh901-debug/gsafsdfsdf) contained the Cyb3rx admin controller APK, with a hardcoded api_base_url pointing to 64.89.163[.]3, exposing endpoints for SMS forwarding control, device removal, phishing data retrieval, and C2 command dispatch (send_command_to_device.php).
- Defanged C2 infrastructure includes 64.89.163[.]3, 78.159.156[.]74, 144.31.244[.]184, 46.151.182[.]28, pool.fud2026[.]com:9000, and install-update[.]xyz. Phishing domains include cancelcardprotection[.]online, deactivatecpservice[.]in, and managecp[.]co[.]in. The report lists SHA256 hashes for samples across all 7 families plus a full IOC table with phishing domains, C2 addresses, and malicious GitHub account names.
Hunt angle: on Android enterprise or MDM-enrolled devices, look for APKs installed outside the Play Store paired with accessibility service grants and SMS READ/SEND permissions, especially where a foreground service persists alongside outbound connections to Firebase or the fud2026[.]com infrastructure. For network defenders, flag DNS or HTTP traffic to pool.fud2026[.]com, fud2026[.]xyz, install-update[.]xyz, and app2-update2[.]site. Full IOCs, hashes, and phishing domain lists are in the report.

item.title: n0n Ransomware: Inside an AI-Assisted Extortion Operation
item.description:
AI-assisted extortion operation n0n hit 93 victims, demanded $283.7M total, and ran its entire attack toolkit through a $7,000+ LLM coding agent. An exposed staging server handed researchers the full playbook.
Key findings:
- STRU found a Python HTTP file server at 185.157.161[.]148:8877 with 1,719 files from the operator's live workspace, including 829 scripts, 5 C++ encryptor sources, and an opencode AI coding agent configured with 154 model entries across seven providers. The agent, which included "uncensored" and "abliterated" models with safety training removed, produced and debugged hundreds of attack scripts with $7,216 in documented gateway spend. No CVEs appeared anywhere in the toolkit: every intrusion relied on weak or stolen credentials, specifically credential stuffing against 305 FortiGate SSL-VPN appliances via residential proxies (watch /remote/logincheck for Cookie: APBSID=n0n), exposed AWS IAM keys, weak RDP/WinRM credentials, and reused hosting portal sessions. MITRE T1110.004, T1078, T1078.004, T1133.
- The encryptor is a lightweight AES-256-CBC locker with Windows, Linux and PowerShell variants, plus an OpenSSL stage for firewall appliances. Each build uses a single hardcoded key with no per-victim key derivation, and the report assesses one key is likely reused across two victims: a decryptor built for one could unlock the other. Wrapper scripts handle the destructive work before encryption runs: services stopped (MSSQL, MySQL, IIS via T1489), shadow copies deleted, free space wiped (T1490), and in some cases provider-hosted backups deleted entirely (T1485). Offline or immutable backups are the only reliable recovery path.
- The most operationally disruptive case: n0n compromised a Venezuelan ISP through its Cisco Firepower Management Center, flipped every access policy to BLOCK via the FMC REST API, and claimed to have severed national network traffic. On Dediserve, stolen admin browser credentials gave full cloud hosting access, tenant backups were extracted, and the Linux locker variant was deployed. On Fanatics, an exposed AWS key led to exfiltration from 40 S3 buckets and deletion of a bank-transaction archive and twelve buckets (CloudTrail pattern: ListBuckets, sustained GetObject, DeleteObjects in 1,000-item batches, PutObject writing n0n_READ_ME.txt). Persistence used SYSTEM scheduled tasks under C:\Users\Public\n0n\ named [NAME]Sync, [NAME]Audit, NetAssist, ChromeDbg, and a Registry Run key n0nNote, plus hidden local admins svc_upd and svc_reg with SpecialAccounts\UserList=0 (T1547.001, T1136.001, T1564.002).
- C2 used HTTPS implants (c2srv[.]py, kserver panel) with status beacons disguised as card-payment JSON POSTed to /x/i containing "ippay-web". Exfiltration ran as zip-base64 POSTs to /c2/.../out with 8 GiB per-target budgets. The infrastructure segments into four nodes: agent box at 185.157.161[.]148, loot vault at 81.161.239[.]10, leak backend at 188.214.135[.]130, and an SSH pivot at 198.13.158[.]143. The beacon cover domain is ntpsync[.]io. All 55 collected Bitcoin addresses showed zero transactions as of October 16, 2026, suggesting no ransoms paid.
Hunt now across EDR for C:\Users\Public\n0n\ creation, *.n0n and n0n_READ_ME files, and rapid renames following MSSQL/W3SVC/MySQL termination. In CloudTrail, flag ssm:SendCommand from new or inactive keys and DeleteObjects sequences. On FortiGate, alert on /remote/logincheck volume with Cookie: APBSID=n0n. For FMC, flag REST token creation from non-management IPs and any default policy flip to BLOCK. The SHA-256 hashes for nenc.cpp (d1fd3a8ac4ada74b8ccbcdf5134797acff401b7fb50e16549b337781dfe1a486), nenc2.cpp (340172627cdf40927784956be784bd2b3f5d1584cb79cf31064f387bbe9acb28), and nenc2l.cpp (886b3608d05069d314fa6300404de6627f96b13a95c5633f6c91dfc2a545ac87), plus the full IOC table and ransom wallet addresses, are in the SOCRadar whitepaper.

item.title: INJ3CTOR3 Malware Steals FreePBX Credentials, Enabling Toll Fraud After Cleanup
item.description:
INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now exfiltrates SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials before cleanup, meaning wiping an infected host no longer stops the toll fraud.
Key findings:
- CRIL documented the JOMANGY PHP webshell in May and analyzed artifacts from INJ3CTOR3's staging servers on 9 September 2026. The updated k.php script ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each containing 17 curl commands that continuously upload FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix config files to /hima_data/index.php on two C2 hosts: 160.119.69[.]4 (plain-text commands) and 45.95.147[.]178 (base64-encoded commands). A cron beacon reruns k.php every minute. If a victim rotates passwords while still infected, the fresh credentials leak within minutes and attackers can register a stolen SIP trunk with the carrier from any location, placing calls that never touch the victim's PBX.
- INJ3CTOR3 has deliberately rotated every indicator defenders were previously told to hunt. The April watermark trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea is now per-build values: trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e. The shared JOMANGY/ZenharR gate hash moved from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. The /x takeover script grew from 367 to 620 lines, primarily to evict rival actors' implants and SSH keys. The panel can also forge a FreePBX admin session through the ampuser class and setAdmin(), so changing the admin password alone does not evict the attacker.
- Two persistence mechanisms are designed to survive log review and console inspection. An .htaccess file planted in /var/www/html/admin/views/ routes requests containing %20 or %09 to config.php, so access logs record only the requested path and a name-based search for the webshell returns nothing. Trunks written directly to /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf are invisible in the FreePBX GUI; they only appear via Asterisk CLI commands such as "pjsip show endpoints". Shadowserver counted over 900 compromised instances in February 2026 and over 700 still infected in May.
- CVE-2025-57819 is the current exploitation vector. Sangoma's patch blocks new entry but does not clean already-compromised systems. CRIL recommends isolating the host first, then preserving crontabs, logs, and the ampusers table before any removal. Removal order matters: cron entries and the zen2 watchdog first, then eight crontab backups and login stagers, then extra UID-0 accounts and accounts carrying $1$nRz1Cbtk$ password hashes, then 12 webshell copies and the freepbxusers row. Credential rotation across all 17 config files comes last. CRIL's begle[.]sh script supports triage.
Takeaway: Do not rotate credentials before completing forensic preservation and full removal. Because INJ3CTOR3 actively rotates hashes and C2 hosts, pivot detection to behavior: cron entries executing PHP scripts at one-minute intervals, outbound curl from a web process, and unexpected rows in the ampusers table. Run "pjsip show endpoints" from the Asterisk CLI and diff against the FreePBX console to surface hidden trunks. IOCs and the full remediation sequence are in CRIL's report.

item.title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
item.description:
INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now exfiltrates credentials every minute, meaning rebuilding an infected host no longer ends exposure. Stolen SIP trunk secrets let the operator call as you from anywhere.
Key details:
- The September build of k.php added credential theft that was absent in April. On every run (cron fires it every minute), it executes 17 curl commands uploading FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix config files covering chan_sip, PJSIP, AMI, the PBX database, and the Postfix SMTP relay account to /hima_data/index.php on both staging hosts: 45.95.147[.]178 and 160.119.69[.]4. Rotating credentials on a still-infected host hands the new secrets to the operator within minutes.
- The operator rotated every identifier defenders had. The JOMANGY webshell gate hash moved from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a (shared with ZenharR), the per-host watermarks are now trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e, and 160.119.69[.]4 was added for plain-text commands while base64-encoded channels still reach 45.95.147[.]178. Hunts seeded from the May report now miss active infections.
- A seven-line .htaccess written to /var/www/html/admin/views/ creates an access-log gap that matters forensically. Requests with an encoded space, tab, or newline (%20, %09, %0A) immediately after a slash return 200 from config.php without that filename appearing in the access log. The takeover script also truncates then deletes the web server, Asterisk, cron, and audit logs and clears shell and MySQL histories, so log hunting is secondary and the credential upload itself leaves no file on disk.
- The /x takeover script grew from 367 to 620 lines, mostly adding cleanup of rival actors' implants and SSH keys. The backdoor account password hash prefix $1$nRz1Cbtk$ is unchanged, as are the eight immutable crontab spares hidden in dot-paths (including /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority and /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache), the /root/.bash_profile and /etc/rc.local stagers, and the encoding chain (base64, base64, ROT13). - Cyble's report maps 19 MITRE ATT&CK techniques including T1552.001, T1119, and T1041, which are new in this generation and describe the credential grab. Three techniques the previous report lacked now cover automated collection and exfiltration over the C2 channel.
Takeaway: Do not rotate credentials before the host is clean, and do not stop at the two known staging hosts when scoping the block. Audit the Asterisk CLI directly (pjsip show registrations, sip show registry) and compare against the FreePBX console because trunks written to /etc/asterisk/*_custom.conf never appear there. Hunt for outbound HTTP POSTs to any /hima_data/ path, cron children that download and pipe to a shell, and any .htaccess under the web root that no installed package or team member placed. The beagle[.]sh triage script is at github[.]com/0x1da5/malware-campaigns and makes no changes to the host. IOCs, hashes, and ATT&CK mappings are in the report.

item.title: Hackers bury inboxes in spam then show up on Microsoft Teams posing as IT support
item.description:
Vishing-over-Teams is now a full production pipeline. Arctic Wolf documented 400+ incidents where attackers bombed inboxes with spam, then posed as IT support on Microsoft Teams to deploy ransomware.
Key findings:
- The attack abuses Microsoft Teams' external access (federation), which is enabled by default across Microsoft 365 tenants. No CVE is involved. Attackers spin up free onmicrosoft[.]com tenants or paid .top and .com domains in minutes, giving them names like "helpdeskteam365" or "itcoreportal", then add display names such as "IT Service Desk (Matthew)" or prefix them with "(Internal)" to impersonate internal staff. Arctic Wolf flagged that 100+ fake identities used emoji like shields and wrenches in display names, possibly suggesting AI-assisted identity generation at scale.
- The attack chain is fast and deliberate. Inbox flooding with newsletter and subscription confirmations arrives first, creating urgency. The Teams message follows minutes later. If the target engages, the attacker pivots to a voice call and requests remote access via Quick Assist (a built-in Windows tool), AnyDesk, or ScreenConnect. Secondary remote-access tools are often installed as a persistence fallback. From first Teams contact to malicious code execution: under 15 minutes in documented cases.
- Attackers deliberately avoid posting links inside Teams, where they would be scanned. Instead, they download malicious files themselves during the remote session. In one documented case, the target was instructed to run a PowerShell command that triggered a hidden script chain. The final payload was a Python implant that enumerated all user and computer account names and descriptions from Active Directory and exfiltrated that data to attacker-controlled servers.
- This TTP is not new but is clearly scaling. Microsoft first documented Teams-based initial access in mid-2024 tied to Black Basta. Arctic Wolf now links the same vector to Cactus, 3AM, and Chaos ransomware operations. The Chaos group's shift from onmicrosoft[.]com tenants toward .top domains mirrors a parallel shift Sophos observed in that campaign. The 400+ incident count in this report alone indicates the technique has moved from targeted use to broad, automated campaigns.
- Forensic timing matters here. In some intrusions, credential theft alerts fired simultaneously with the first Teams chat alert, meaning the endpoint was already compromised before any analyst looked at it. Responders should not assume the Teams chat is the start of the timeline: scope the investigation backward, check for prior PowerShell execution, staged script drops, and any remote access tool installs that preceded or coincided with the first alert.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull Microsoft Teams external access logs and filter for chats from onmicrosoft[.]com tenants and .top or unknown domains contacting your users. Cross-reference timestamps with inbox spike events, Quick Assist or AnyDesk process creation, and any PowerShell spawning from user-context sessions. If Quick Assist is not used by your IT team, its execution should be a high-priority alert. The report recommends restricting external Teams federation to named partner domains only and blocking unmanaged and trial tenant access entirely.

item.title: Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes
item.description:
Microsoft Teams external chat is being weaponized at scale: over 400 observed incidents where attackers impersonating IT support reached payload execution in under 15 minutes, with ransomware-linked groups including Black Basta among known adopters of this vector.
Key findings:
- The attack chain combines mail bombing (hundreds of newsletter/subscription confirmations flooding the target's inbox), followed immediately by a Teams message from a fake "IT Service Desk" account offering to fix the problem the attacker just created. The entire sequence from first contact to remote access takes under 15 minutes, and the targeting of multiple victims in short windows points to automation driving the volume.
- Attacker infrastructure leans on legitimacy by design. Between 30-40% of cases used default onmicrosoft[.]com tenant domains, which require no verification and can be provisioned in minutes. Tenant names were themed around support, IT, admin, network, or helpdesk, sometimes suffixed with "365", and display names mimicked real staff (e.g. "IT Service Desk - Liam"). In a small number of cases, the target organization's own name appeared in the sender tenant to add credibility.
- Teams external access is enabled by default across Microsoft 365, meaning any external tenant can initiate chat with your users without additional configuration. This is the structural enabler: attackers need no foothold, no phishing email delivered to inbox, and no malicious attachment to begin the social engineering chain.
- Once voice or chat contact is established, the primary pivot is Quick Assist, the RMM tool built into Windows that requires no installation and leaves a lower alert footprint. When attackers need persistence beyond that initial session, they drop commercial RMM tools such as AnyDesk and ScreenConnect. From there, PowerShell payload execution and lateral movement follow, with ransomware deployment documented in some cases.
- The forensic trail to chase: look for Quick Assist sessions (msra.exe or quickassist.exe) launched during business hours shortly after a user reports inbox flooding. Correlate with Teams external chat logs for messages from onmicrosoft[.]com tenants with support- or helpdesk-themed names. Pivot to any AnyDesk or ScreenConnect installs that followed within the same session window, and pull PowerShell script block logging for commands executed under those RMM parent processes.
Practitioner takeaway: Lock down Teams external access now. In the Teams admin center under Users > External access, switch from "Allow all external domains" to an allowlist of known partner domains only. Block federation with unmanaged and trial-only tenants. Restrict or remove Quick Assist from non-IT endpoints via policy. For hunting, correlate mail flow anomalies (sudden subscription confirmation spikes) with Teams external chat session records and RMM process launches in the same timeframe. The Arctic Wolf report contains additional defender recommendations and observed TTPs.

item.title: Locked and Loaded: Phishing through Fake Bids and Protected Documents
item.description:
Credential phishing campaign weaponizes fake bid invitations and password-protected PDFs to bypass email security gateways, harvesting Microsoft credentials through a multi-stage lure chain built on legitimate-looking business workflows.
Key findings:
- The attack opens with a spoofed "Project Bid Invitation" email, potentially sent from a previously compromised legitimate account to strip away the most obvious red flag: a suspicious sender domain. The attached PDF (MM LASERTECHNIK GMBH_protected.pdf, SHA256: 9ca705d6466d4d71c3fb0cae5097933afe1de1bc139d53bb63565a52dc9ebccb, MD5: c9281ea6828b9de4443ac56361ac29da, 56776 bytes) is password-protected, a deliberate choice because encrypted files are opaque to most email security scanners that rely on content inspection.
- Inside the unlocked PDF sits a single OneDrive-branded button. The underlying URL resolves to hXXps://slotpastimaxwin50jt[.]online/autoproject@autoproject[.]com/index[.]php (IP: 67.205.150[.]245), a redirector that leads to a fake shared document drive mimicking a real contract file listing, keeping the victim inside the bid narrative.
- The fake drive prompts a checkbox file selection and a "Download Selected" action, then pops a window requesting the victim's email address, a pattern borrowed directly from legitimate document-sharing platforms to normalize credential entry before the phishing page even loads.
- The final credential harvesting page impersonates Microsoft sign-in at hXXps://mm-lasertechnik.lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/1Dmw9/?key=NKsIDYXvtY (IPs: 104.21.82[.]118, 172.67.157[.]109). Submitted email and password are exfiltrated to hXXps://nbpn.lastingonlineexperiences[.]de/nasa[.]php, completing the credential theft. The full chain: phishing email, encrypted PDF, redirector, fake drive, fake login, exfil endpoint, is five hops deep before credentials are stolen.
DFIR takeaway: If you are triaging a potential compromise from this campaign, the PDF attachment is your Stage 1 artifact. Pull it for hash verification against the indicators above, and check mail gateway logs for the password-protected PDF delivery pattern alongside bid-themed subject lines. For account exposure, look for Microsoft 365 sign-in events originating from unexpected IPs or locations shortly after the lure email was received: that is your earliest post-compromise signal. IOCs for all stages are listed in the report.

item.title: FortiBleed 2.0: 975 New Domains & 40,573 Exposed Secrets: Claim Your Ethical Disclosure
item.description:
FortiBleed 2.0 surfaces 40,573 cleartext secrets from 1,703 FortiGate configuration files dated February 2026, exposing LDAP bind accounts, VPN credentials, HA cluster secrets, and admin logins across 975 domains not seen in the first disclosure.
Key findings:
- The 101,419-record CSV breaks down into 37,076 cleartext local-user and SSL-VPN entries, 1,576 cleartext Active Directory LDAP bind passwords, 1,672 administrator logins labeled FortiGate_Super_Admin_Verified_Login in the source export, 208 HA cluster records (144 cleartext), and 176 SMTP relay records (105 cleartext). Another 10,743 records carry undecrypted FortiOS ENC values, which may be recoverable offline when the system-default key was used rather than a device-specific private-data-encryption key. CVE-2026-24858 (CVSS 9.4) is named in the campaign context; Fortinet issued its advisory January 27, 2026, before the February 20 report timestamps. Related research ties victim overlap to Qilin and The Gentlemen, though a direct affiliation with threat actor k0t remains unconfirmed.
- The associated toolchain, documented by NyxLab under the k0t investigation, chains three stages: forti_parse.py extracts and decrypts configuration material; vpn_checker.py combined with openconnect attempts VPN sessions using recovered local-user credentials; nxc/NetExec is then used against internal systems using LDAP bind identities. An overprivileged bind account can expose far more than the firewall itself, but ordinary LDAP query rights alone do not grant domain-admin access, replication rights, or NTDS.dit access.
- Of the 765 host identifiers overlapping with FortiBleed 1.0, 524 (68.4%) show identical username and cleartext password pairs across both datasets, meaning those credentials were not rotated between the two collection periods. The remaining 242 records show different administrator usernames on the same hosts. Recurring account names to investigate include fgtsecure (106 occurrences with a recurring password pattern), fgtsec, Technical_support, forticloud-sync, forti-auth-tech, callcenter, districtadmin, and fortiadmin. In 89.3% of differing-login cases, both the old and new admin accounts coexist in the February configuration, giving responders a concrete list of accounts to reconcile against change history.
- Attribution is complicated by MSSP and IT contractor registration email addresses masking the true victim organization. The report documents three examples: 203.159.253[.]220 registered to nti[.]co[.]th but attributed to ovec.go[.]th; 211.75.64[.]189 registered to jp[.]ricoh[.]com but attributed to elumax[.]com; 49.229.69[.]162 registered to dataworkconnect[.]com but attributed to ads.payap[.]ac[.]th. Perimeter list membership alone does not identify the end organization.
DFIR takeaway: Affected organizations should pull config system admin, config user ldap, config user local, config system ha, and config system email-server from their FortiGate backup and compare every account name against the recurring patterns named above (fgtsecure, Technical_support, forticloud-sync, forti-auth-tech, callcenter) using configuration history and ownership records. LDAP bind accounts need immediate secret rotation and privilege review, and the LDAP server addresses in the export should be reconciled against directory authentication logs for lateral movement. The Hudson Rock report notes IOCs and exposure records are indexed in their free portal at hudsonrock[.]com/fortinet for domain lookups and ethical disclosure requests.

item.title: How to Export Firewall Logs from Palo Alto and FortiGate
item.description:
Firewall logs are only as good as the logging config behind them. PAN-OS and FortiGate both ship with critical gaps that leave denied traffic and admin activity invisible unless you fix them first.
Key findings:
- The most common collection failure is not a tool problem, it is a policy problem. On PAN-OS, the predefined intrazone-default and interzone-default rules do not log by default, meaning denied traffic that falls through to them leaves no record. On FortiGate, logging is configured per policy and the implicit deny policy is silent by default. Before you pull any logs for an investigation, verify what was actually being logged during the window that matters.
- On-box history is limited and volatile. Smaller FortiGate models without a disk log only to memory, which a reboot wipes entirely. If Panorama, Strata Logging Service, FortiAnalyzer, or FortiCloud are in the environment, start there, they almost certainly hold more history than the firewall itself.
- The recommended collection path is syslog forwarding to a Linux collector running rsyslog. The report walks through a minimal rsyslog config writing to /var/log/firewall/fw.log, listening on UDP 514. On PAN-OS, attach the Log Forwarding profile to security rules and separately forward System and Config logs under Device, Log Settings. On FortiGate CLI, the config log syslogd setting block enables forwarding. Once in place, grep by date to carve a time slice for analysis.
- For existing on-box history, FortiGate's GUI (Log & Report, then the relevant category) supports raw log download in text, CSV, or JSON. GUI downloads are capped, typically 400,000 entries on-device or 2,000 to 40,000 via FortiGate Cloud. Larger pulls require the CLI command execute backup disk/memory alllogs ftp/tftp.
- Do not overlook admin-plane logs. System and Config logs on PAN-OS and event logs on FortiGate record admin logins and configuration changes. Edge devices are now a primary entry point, and "who logged into the firewall at 3 a.m. and what did they change" is a legitimate forensic question with its own log source.
Practitioner takeaway: before treating absent log data as absence of activity, audit the logging policy itself. On PAN-OS, confirm logging is enabled on the default and implicit deny rules and that the Log Forwarding profile is committed and attached. On FortiGate, check each policy's logging setting. If the collector is receiving nothing, run tcpdump -n udp port 514 on the collector to isolate whether the gap is network, config, or rsyslog. Patterns worth hunting in the exported data: repeated outbound sessions to a rare external IP at regular intervals (beaconing), a single internal host sending disproportionate outbound bytes (exfiltration), and many destination ports from one source in a short window (scanning).

item.title: Lazarus Abuses South Korean Security Software to Deploy Malware Using Post-Quantum Encryption
item.description:
North Korean 🇰🇵 Lazarus Group's Operation FlashHole abuses mandatory South Korean 🇰🇷 financial security software INISAFE CrossWeb EX to deliver a multi-stage, fully in-memory malware framework protected by post-quantum encryption, active since at least July 2025.
Key findings:
- The attack chain exploits Initech's INISAFE CrossWeb EX, a certificate authentication tool installed on virtually every South Korean 🇰🇷 banking and government-portal machine, to abuse the legitimate Windows binary fsquirt.exe via DLL sideloading. A malicious DLL called TechHub loads entirely in memory, downloads TouchHub from GitHub, which sideloads TOUCHSHIFT (disguised as mscoree.dll) for persistence, then chains into ClientHub and LPEClient before landing Cubridge, the framework's orchestration engine. The entire initial compromise exists only in memory, leaving minimal on-disk artifacts to recover.
- The malware stack is a generational evolution of known Lazarus tooling. TechHub advances CLOUDBURST/NickelLoader. Cubridge is an improved SIDESHOW/LightlessCan and also assessed as an advanced CookiePlus variant. ClientHub is previously undocumented and comes in two versions: one using HTTPS C2 and one interacting with the Dropbox API. LPEClient, in use since 2019, profiles victims and delivers payloads. Cubridge pulls reusable plugins capable of ZIP archiving, file collection by search pattern, file deletion, and local drive change monitoring.
- The standout technical development is LPEClient's adoption of ML-KEM-1024, a post-quantum cryptographic algorithm, to encrypt C2 communications before downloading and executing additional malware in memory. Kaspersky traces this capability back to at least September 2024, meaning Lazarus has been running quantum-resistant comms for over a year before this disclosure. This directly degrades any passive decryption or SSL inspection capability defenders relied on.
- In at least one confirmed FlashHole-linked intrusion, COPPERHEDGE (also tracked as Brandoor) resulted in data exfiltration to a dark web leak site named ULOSE, mirroring Gunra ransomware extortion tactics against South Korean 🇰🇷 targets at the same period. This blurs the line between espionage and financially motivated extortion and widens the impact classification. Operation FlashHole is assessed by Kaspersky as the latest wave of the broader Cascade Hole campaign.
- Initial lure infrastructure included malicious GitHub Pages hosting AI-generated profile photos and fabricated senior network developer resumes, used in targeted spearphishing to direct victims to sites that trigger the CrossWeb EX exploit chain. This continues Lazarus's pattern from Operation SyncHole (Cross EX exploitation) and Operation Double Barrel (AnySign4PC exploitation flagged in a joint July 2026 KISA advisory).
DFIR takeaway: On any South Korean 🇰🇷 endpoint running INISAFE CrossWeb EX, hunt for fsquirt.exe spawned by INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe and any DLL loaded from unusual paths by that process. Because the chain runs in memory, focus on injected threads in fsquirt.exe and SyncHost.exe, and look for mscoree.dll loaded from non-standard locations. LPEClient's ML-KEM-1024 C2 traffic will resist decryption at the perimeter, so detections need to pivot to behavioral indicators: unusual GitHub-directed network calls from sideloaded DLLs and Dropbox API traffic from processes that have no business reaching it. The full technical breakdown and malware family details are in Kaspersky's report.

item.title: Responder Guidance for PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
item.description:
Two critical unauthenticated RCE flaws in PHP's core engine (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) affect every PHP install serving web requests, regardless of application. Public PoCs are circulating and Bishop Fox confirmed RCE in their lab with ASLR enabled.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory corruption triggered by flooding PHP's multipart POST parser with a large number of per-part header lines. The OOM interrupts parsing while internal structures like the $_POST array are partially initialized, and request cleanup then treats that invalid data as valid, handing an attacker a corrupted-memory primitive. On mod_php this fires before any application code runs. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free in PHP's serializer state: a request that dies mid-flight (attacker-induced fatal error or timeout) can strand stale, freed state that a subsequent worker request reuses before per-request initialization resets it. The confirmed delivery path rides session.upload_progress, a default-on engine feature. Both are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
- Exploitation scope is every SAPI: mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed are all in scope. Risk is highest under mod_php, where a single unauthenticated request triggers both bugs pre-application. On PHP-FPM and php-cgi the direct OOM path produces a worker crash and respawn (denial of service) rather than RCE, but the vendor still considers all SAPIs at risk and an application-dependent RCE path exists on FPM. Bishop Fox confirmed full unauthenticated RCE with ASLR enabled against stock php:8.3, php:8.4, and php:8.5 Apache mod_php Docker images.
- The CVE-2026-109619 public session chain leaks memory addresses out of a PHP error message printed into the HTTP response during request parsing, using that one-shot leak to defeat ASLR. Setting display_errors = Off before any application ini_set removes that leak and forces an attacker to blind brute-force. On Apache prefork, every respawned worker inherits the parent's memory layout, making ASLR constant per master and giving a brute-force attacker a stable, repeatable target.
- Partial mitigations that raise the bar without replacing a patch: set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config (not via ini_set or .user.ini) to remove the confirmed CVE-2026-109619 delivery vector; set memory_limit = -1 and enforce it via a container or cgroup boundary that kills only the affected worker (not RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which reintroduce the allocation failure); cap post_max_size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth at the proxy or web server layer; set fatal_error_backtraces = 0 on PHP 8.5 to block the confirmed fatal-backtrace trigger for CVE-2026-109619. None of these is a substitute for patching.
Responder takeaway: version alone tells you a host is exposed but not how exploitable it is. Inventory every PHP host and prioritize mod_php deployments, EOL branches (7.4, 8.0, 8.1), and hosts with display_errors = On or session.upload_progress enabled, as those present the cleanest attack surface. Hunt for bursts of worker crashes or respawns in Apache and FPM logs as a signal of active exploitation attempts, particularly on ARM where blind brute-force produces detectable crash bursts. Patch to the fixed versions listed above and restart every worker after any change. The Bishop Fox report details the confirmed attack chains and interim mitigations.

item.title: Where to Find Windows DNS Server Logs
item.description:
Windows DNS Server logs to four distinct locations, most disabled by default. Knowing where each lives and what it captures is the difference between a complete timeline and a dead end during an active investigation.
Key findings:
- The Audit channel (Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Audit) is on by default and records zone and record changes: creation, deletion, and modification. This is your first stop for record hijacking, such as a rogue wpad entry being added outside a change window. Export it with: wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Audit" C:\logs\dns_audit.evtx. The Analytical channel captures every query and response but is off by default and hidden until you enable View > Show Analytic and Debug Logs in Event Viewer. Enable it going forward with: wevtutil sl "Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Analytical" /e:true. If you are responding to something that already happened and Analytical was never enabled, there are no server-side query logs to recover from this source.
- When server-side query logs are absent, pivot to client-side and network sources: Sysmon event 22 on endpoints, the DNS Client event log, firewall or proxy logs, or a network sensor. These are your retrospective options. Sysmon event 22 adds process attribution the DNS server log never provides, since the server only records the client IP, not the process that made the request.
- The debug log at C:\Windows\System32\dns\dns.log is a plain-text file enabled through DNS Manager > server Properties > Debug Logging. It carries more packet detail than the Analytical channel but overwrites itself when it hits its size limit, which means it may already be gone if the incident is not fresh. Collect it with: copy C:\Windows\System32\dns\dns.log C:\logs\. A plugin DLL loaded by the DNS Server service is also worth examining: DnsAdmins group abuse can drop a malicious DLL that runs as SYSTEM.
- On the investigation side, hunt for: very long or high-entropy subdomains (DNS tunneling, T1071.004), single clients generating high NXDOMAIN volumes (domain-generation algorithm activity, T1568.002), and elevated TXT query rates from one host (C2 or data exfil over DNS). Audit log events for record changes outside approved windows point to record hijacking or internal reconnaissance.
- A practical note on collection: Get-WinEvent against the Analytical channel requires the -Oldest flag or it will error. Event Viewer may require you to disable the Analytical log before it displays events. The debug log and EVTX files contain internal hostnames and client IPs. Treat them as sensitive before routing to any external or shared analysis platform.
Takeaway: Before anything else, check whether the Analytical channel was enabled on your DNS server. If it was not, note the gap in your timeline and shift to Sysmon event 22, DNS Client logs, and network sensor data for retrospective query visibility. Enable Analytical logging now to close the gap going forward, and set up log forwarding so the debug log does not silently roll over during your next investigation.
