item.title: CVE-2026-35273: SSRF to RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft
item.description:
CVE-2026-35273 is an SSRF-to-RCE chain in Oracle PeopleSoft under active mass exploitation by ShinyHunters, patched in September 2026 but still burning through unpatched internet-facing deployments.
Key findings:
- The attack chain starts with an unauthenticated POST to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector, specifying HttpTargetConnector and setting the target URL to hxxp://127.0.0.1:8000. The HttpTargetConnector handler (ZDI-CAN-31816) performs zero validation on the destination, forwarding the full attacker-controlled payload to the loopback interface. Oracle's validateClient logic in PSEMHUB checks the requesting host against allowedhosts[.]properties, which ships with localhost trusted by default, so a loopback-sourced request passes straight through. The SSRF exists precisely because the Integration Gateway and the Hub are two separate WebLogic applications with no shared trust boundary.
- Once inside PSEMHUB, the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler (ZDI-CAN-31818) exposes an External Control of File Path. The m_line parameter holds arbitrary file contents and m_targetFile holds an absolute path, with no validation that the destination is a legitimate log directory. Attackers used this to write JSP web shells directly into the PSEMHUB WAR path, achieving RCE as the PeopleSoft service account immediately on the next HTTP request to that path.
- A stealthier persistence path (ZDI-CAN-31817) abuses Java XMLDecoder deserialization. Any file write primitive, including the one above, lets an attacker drop a malicious XML file into the docroot/envmetadata/data/environment/ directory. On the next PSEMHUB HubServlet initialization, the class calls HubMBeanPersistance.getInstance(), iterates every file in that directory, instantiates XMLDecoder, and deserializes the attacker's payload before the expected type cast even throws an exception. This path drops no JSP shell, making it harder to catch with standard web shell detection.
- ShinyHunters attribution came from Mandiant's September 25, 2026 report documenting continued mass exploitation. The three bugs were reported to Oracle on June 10, 2026 under a single CVE, with separate CVE assignments coordinated but not yet issued. Any internet-facing PeopleSoft instance that has not applied Oracle's patch is a live target right now.
Practitioner takeaway: Start triage at the PSIGW access logs and look for POST requests to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector where the payload body contains a loopback address (127.0.0.1 or localhost) in the target URL field. Then audit the PSEMHUB WAR directory for unexpected JSP files and the docroot/envmetadata/data/environment/ directory for XML files you did not place there. For post-exploitation, review process trees spawned under the PeopleSoft service account for shells or recon commands. The deserialization path is triggered at service restart, so check whether any restarts were recorded around the time suspicious XML appeared. Apply Oracle's patch and review allowedhosts[.]properties to confirm localhost is not silently exposing PSEMHUB to untrusted connectors in your environment.

item.title: Patched, Not Over: PHP2Shell Exploits Keep Spreading Underground
item.description:
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS 9.2 each) hit PHP core at the web server layer. Patches shipped Oct 21, but exploit code kept circulating on underground forums through Oct 23.
- Both flaws are memory-safety bugs in PHP core: CVE-2026-109618 covers invalid state after an out-of-memory interruption, CVE-2026-109619 covers stale global state persisting across requests. PHP's own disclosure includes a demonstrated Apache mod_php exploit path that fires before any application code runs, putting every PHP deployment serving web traffic in scope. Unit 42 estimates more than 22.6 million potentially exposed instances. Fixed versions are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. A separate third flaw, CVE-2026-115560, a configuration-dependent RCE tied to session upload progress, was noticed on Oct 23 and is distinct from the two original CVEs. PHP recommends disabling session.upload_progress.enabled until the next bugfix release.
- Exploitation is not theoretical. watchTowr's honeypots recorded active exploitation attempts on Oct 21, the same day patches dropped. VulnCheck links scanning to 85.11.167[.]243 and 45.198.224[.]169. Arctic Wolf links the domains thunder.godofthunder[.]st and godofthunder[.]st to Potassium samples, and observed attempted retrieval of /nfs-setup from 92.118.112[.]100, though payload execution was not confirmed. An inbound scanner hit alone does not confirm RCE: prioritize hosts where scanning coincides with suspicious child processes or unexpected files.
- Underground circulation after the patch is the signal defenders should not dismiss. ThreatMon reviewed 13 observations across English, Russian 🇷🇺, and Turkish 🇹🇷 forums and Persian-language Telegram channels. A php2shell[.]py download offer appeared Oct 23, a "Full Exploit Source" archive posted Oct 22 cited the fixed PHP versions in the same message, and a claimed local RCE with www-data command output appeared Oct 22. No independently verified customer compromise was found, but the mix of download offers and PoC redistribution shows sustained attacker interest.
- The most reliable post-exploitation signal is a PHP or web server process doing something it never normally does. The ThreatMon report describes five hunt categories: web server processes (php-fpm, php-cgi, php, lsphp, apache2, httpd, nginx, w3wp.exe) spawning shells or interpreters; post-exploitation recon commands such as whoami, id, uname, curl, wget, or inline php -r; PHP files created or modified by web processes in the web directory; PHP worker segfaults and core dumps; and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS requests paired with memory-exhaustion errors. The full report ships 28 queries covering Carbon Black EDR, Splunk, Elasticsearch, QRadar, and Microsoft Sentinel.
Confirm the running runtime version separately from the CLI version, because container images and bundled runtimes often lag behind OS packages. The ThreatMon report includes the full 28-query detection set, 20 IPs, 4 domains, and 3 URLs as IOCs. Preserve EDR process trees, web request logs, PHP error logs, and any files created in /tmp or /dev/shm before removing exclusions or rotating logs.

item.title: php2shell in Practice: Exploitable, Conditional, and Hard to Mass-Exploit
item.description:
php2shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619): pre-auth RCE in PHP core is confirmed exploitable but heavily conditional, with real-world mass exploitation unlikely due to version-specific offsets, heap precision requirements, and configuration dependencies.
Key findings:
- Two pre-auth RCE bugs affect PHP core. CVE-2026-109618 targets the dangling PS session global via mod_php (Apache) and the php -S dev server. CVE-2026-109619 involves the serializer and hits PHP-FPM. Public exploits have focused almost entirely on the mod_php path. Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Citrix NetScaler have both published advisories confirming impact, and their management interfaces running Apache with mod_php are notable high-value targets given that management traffic is low-volume, making it easier to land two requests on the same worker as the exploit requires.
- Exploitation of mod_php under the default display_errors=Off setting requires: defeating ASLR via a heap information leak through a stale PS(id) pointer in php_session_rfc1867_callback, version and build-specific binary offsets (compiler flags and distribution builds change the layout), precise heap grooming to exhaust freelist buckets and trigger an OOM exactly inside php_session_send_cookie so PS(send_cookie) stays set to 1, and pairing two requests on the same Apache prefork worker. Crucially, Apache prefork does not re-randomize ASLR on fork, so a successful leak exposes the heap base and libphp addresses for all workers until a restart.
- The display_errors=On exploitation path is substantially easier because an early error causes SG(headers_sent) to be set, which makes php_session_send_cookie fail and leaves PS(send_cookie) = 1 without the precise heap timing. Praetorian found zero live customer-facing hosts with display_errors=On across their exposed phpinfo scan data. That means the easy path is largely theoretical in production, and real exploitation requires the much harder OOM-timed leak.
- Exposed phpinfo pages, typically rated low or informational, are the reconnaissance gift that makes this practical. A single phpinfo response reveals: exact PHP version and build provider (enough to pull a matching Docker image and derive offsets locally), Server API confirming mod_php, display_errors and memory_limit values, and the Apache MPM confirming prefork. Together these let an attacker skip guesswork and confirm whether their offset database applies before sending a single exploit request.
- The flood of non-functional AI-generated PoCs released after the leak illustrates a specific failure mode: models bypassed the vulnerability entirely by enabling display_errors=On in their lab environments or by attempting to brute-force 64-bit ASLR rather than implementing the leak. Defenders should treat public PoC counts as a poor signal of actual exploitability right now. The FPM variant (CVE-2026-109619) has early public exploits but Praetorian has not yet confirmed that exploitation path.
Practitioner takeaway: Pull your external attack surface for exposed phpinfo pages and any management interfaces running PHP. The php_session_rfc1867_callback function and multipart form POST requests with PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS fields in the same session are the behavioral signature of exploitation attempts on the mod_php path. On network logging, watch for repeated large multipart uploads followed immediately by a second request to the same application from the same source: that two-request sequencing is structurally required by the exploit. For PAN-OS and NetScaler specifically, confirm management interfaces are not internet-exposed. Patch to a fixed PHP build and treat any exposed phpinfo finding in pending reports as urgent to remediate now, not at next cycle.

item.title: SkyW4lker Exposed: A Growing Microsoft 365 Phishing Threat to American Enterprises
item.description:
SkyW4lker phishing kit bypasses MFA by abusing Microsoft's device-code OAuth flow, hitting US 🇺🇸 enterprises hard: 618 sandbox analyses logged June through October 2026, with monthly volume jumping from 20 to 200 submissions.
Key findings:
- SkyW4lker is a PHP-plus-JavaScript phishing kit that never needs to steal a password. It directs victims through a chain of decoy pages, eventually asking them to enter a Microsoft device code at login[.]microsoft[.]com/device or login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/deviceauth. The backend polls /assets/php/endpoints/session_public.php?action=poll every few seconds; when authentication completes, the attacker receives a valid OAuth access token (T1528), bypassing MFA entirely. Victim email, password, browser fingerprint, MFA status, and country are also logged via endpoint.js to php/endpoints/accounts.php (T1056.003).
- Delivery starts with a password-protected PDF, DOCX, or XLSX lure (T1566.001), password included in the email body, using business subjects like contracts, invoices, and service proposals (T1656). Intermediate redirect stages abuse Miro, Google Sites, Zoom, Axure Cloud, and Smartsheet to pass reputation checks (T1566.002, T1608.005). A self-hosted CAPTCHA at /assets/private_captcha/public/widget.js?v=4 gates the final phishing page against automated scanners (T1497). JavaScript is obfuscated via obfuscator[.]io (T1027), flagged in 520 of 618 analyses.
- With high confidence, ANY.RUN's report links SkyW4lker to Gabagool, a credential phishing kit first seen April 23, 2026, two months prior. Both kits share client_geo.js, url_helper.js, and endpoint.js modules, the /assets/php/endpoints/confirm_visit.php endpoint, the same self-hosted CAPTCHA path, and landing URL token patterns zt[A-Za-z0-9]{32}op and it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us. They were co-hosted on the same directories across 5200m[.]com/kvme2/, torvion[.]life/ofulium/, and ghethim[.]com/hyllen/ on overlapping dates. Gabagool harvests credentials via accounts.php; SkyW4lker steals tokens via session_public.php: two attack modes, one developer platform.
- Infrastructure leans heavily on DigitalOcean (50 of 92 backend IPs), with notable backend IPs including 162.243.64[.]121 and 67.205.154[.]32, and a shared IP of 172.86.85[.]51 (priorispace[.]biz). Typosquatted Microsoft-themed hostname chains follow patterns like (docshare|sdocshares|pdocshared|efaxdoc|reauth|statement|copilot|login|auth).*(outlook|onedrive|copilot|office365).*. with examples including sdocshares.auth.outlook2026common.copilos26.csr-rooflng[.]com and pdocshared.payments2026.outlooks.common.ecmholdlnggroup[.]com. The report lists 173 domains hosting the kit, plus a full IOC table of URL patterns and backend indicators.
- The administration panel sits at /admin/index.php on the same domain as each kit's backend, protected by MFA via Telegram. CSS class names from command-center.css reveal a dashboard with victim geolocation stats, live visit notifications, link generation, and server management. The report's attribution pivot started from the distinctive /js/url_helper.js, /js/client_geo.js, and /js/endpoint.js paths returning results tagged gabagool in threat intelligence searches.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs for device-code authentication flows that follow receipt of a suspicious attachment or an inbound link from a document-sharing service; device-code grants appearing without a registered device enrollment workflow are a high-confidence signal. In proxy or DNS logs, watch for repeated GET requests to /assets/php/endpoints/session_public.php?action=poll at short intervals originating from a browser session, and flag any outbound resolution to the hostname chain patterns above. The full IOC table of 173 domains, backend IPs, URL patterns, and the single confirmed hash (SHA256 9aa0b87974b9b4cd42603833b7ad44257578467d279b315a071108a5ed02c268 for a lure document) is in the report. If device-code auth is not operationally required, restrict or block it via Microsoft Entra Conditional Access before the next polling cycle beats you to a token.

item.title: SARS tax refund phishing: tracing a global phishing kit
item.description:
Two South African 🇿🇦 Weebly phishing domains led to a dedicated bulletproof server hosting 50 government, bank, and registrar lures across 11 countries, all running the same antibot kit.
Key findings:
- The pivot chain started with justice-gov-za.weebly[.]com and ncpg-gov-za.weebly[.]com, both identified via VMRay UniqueSignal. On shared platforms like Weebly and Cloudflare Pages, IP addresses and wildcard SSL certificates are useless as pivots because thousands of legitimate sites share them. The naming convention, specifically the *-gov-za pattern, was the only selective fingerprint, and a VirusTotal entity:domain query on domain:*gov-za* surfaced the broader cluster.
- A SARS lure at sars-gov-za.vetactivity[.]ro resolved to 46.151.182[.]230 at Ghosty Networks LLC (AS205759), classified as a bulletproof network with prior links to March 2026 malspam campaigns. A urlscan page.ip query on that address returned 372 historical scans and exposed the full multi-country kit: Polish 🇵🇱 tax authority lures (e-Urząd Skarbowy), Iceland's Skatturinn and Íslandsbanki, Lithuania's 🇱🇹 VMI, France's 🇫🇷 Crédit Agricole, Germany's 🇩🇪 ELSTER, UAE's 🇦🇪 e& enterprise, Spanish 🇪🇸 registrars, and an OpenAI checkout credential-harvest page, all sharing the same infrastructure.
- The kit gates every lure behind captcha.html loading antibot.js (SHA-256: 095b95643a6c7ddbe2a70bd28e00556e2c2bf9b4eb83df93074d80fc1c9b60c0) followed by a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge. This bot-evasion flow, mapped to T1497, blocks automated scanners from seeing the phishing content. The same Cloudflare Turnstile sitekey appearing across multiple domains is an operator-linking signal even when the sitekey itself is not searchable. Compromised carrier domains include vetactivity[.]ro, onestaprod[.]ro, clinicaactmedica[.]ro, energy-report[.]ro, and hahn-polyfilms[.]com.
- Distinguishing attacker-owned domains from compromised ones matters for attribution and takedown. A compromised domain shows years of stable apex passive DNS history with only the subdomain diverging recently. An attacker-registered domain has no such split. The report's IOC table applies this test to all 50 lure domains and labels each accordingly, covering hosting providers from Weebly and Cloudflare Pages to Oracle, Amazon, Contabo, and Akamai.
- MITRE coverage in the report: T1583.001 (look-alike domains), T1583.003 (VPS at Ghosty Networks), T1583.006 (Weebly and Cloudflare Pages abuse), T1584.001 (compromised carrier domains), T1566.002 (SMS and email lure delivery), T1656 (brand impersonation), T1497 (antibot evasion), T1598.003 (credential and card harvesting).
Hunt: search proxy logs and urlscan for requests to captcha.html paired with the antibot.js SHA-256 hash above. Block 46.151.182[.]230 and monitor AS205759 for new kit deployments. Alert on newly registered or newly resolving domains matching *-gov-za on any TLD, including *.weebly.com and *.pages.dev subdomains. Full IOC table with 50 lure domains, hosting providers, ownership assessments, and first-seen passive DNS dates is in the report.

item.title: Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries
item.description:
Fake AI desktop apps (GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus) deliver the Yoba malware chain via DLL sideloading against signed OpenAI and Anthropic binaries, with Russian 🇷🇺 origin indicators and a Telegram-seeded DGA for C2.
The Yoba campaign, tracked by Check Point Research, abuses AI hype to lure victims through SEO-poisoned GitHub repositories and GitHub[.]io pages impersonating ChatGPT and Claude releases. The ZIP releases contain legitimate signed binaries alongside a malicious winmm.dll (YobaDropper), which Setup.exe sideloads at runtime. The attacker's OPSEC avoids dedicated C2 infrastructure entirely, routing through Telegram, DNS-over-HTTPS, Catbox, and Tor.
- YobaDropper (winmm.dll) uses DJB2 hashing (seed 0x1505) to verify its host process basename matches 0xE6C2F326 (Setup.exe). A failed check does not terminate but triggers 200,000 iterations of Sleep(5500), stalling analysis for roughly 12.73 days. The dropper also checks keyboard layout against a bitmask (0xEC0400C8401) to exclude CIS-region languages (Russian 🇷🇺, Belarusian 🇧🇾, Kazakh 🇰🇿, Georgian, and others) while explicitly including Ukrainian 🇺🇦 (ID 0x22). If not running as administrator, it prompts the user for elevation and exits. XOR key IRANNUMBERONE decrypts the embedded YobaLoader, which is dropped as wmpdui.dll in ProgramData\WMProcess alongside a copied WMPDMC.exe.

item.title: Process trees in Livehunt: YARA rules that know who launched what
item.description:
VirusTotal's Livehunt YARA module now exposes parent_name and ancestor_names per process, letting hunters write rules that bind a command line to who launched it and what it wrote, closing a gap that flat process lists left open.
Key findings:
- YARA-X v1.21.0 added parent_name to vt.behaviour.processes_list entries, and v1.22.0 added ancestor_names (nearest ancestor first, so ancestor_names[0] equals parent_name and ancestor_names[1] is the grandparent). Every sandbox report that includes a process tree is flattened into this list. Each entry also carries per-process files_written, files_opened, files_deleted, and files_copied, so a rule can now assert that a specific process both ran from a suspicious parent and wrote a specific file class.
- The critical authoring caveat: sandbox process names are not normalized. CAPE quotes the full command line, Zenbox prepends the image path, Tencent HABO gives only the executable name, and some sandboxes leave environment variables unexpanded. Always use icontains on the executable name, never == or startswith on a full path. PID-based linking is equally unreliable because multiple sandboxes share the same processes_list, and PIDs collide across reports. The ancestor_names array is sandbox-scoped, so climbing the tree with it never mixes processes from different sandboxes.
- Five production-tested rules are detailed in the report, each with at least one test hash. The mshta_spawns_shell rule ports Sigma rule 03cc0c25 using p.parent_name icontains "mshta.exe". The dcom_mshta_spawns_shell rule walks to ancestor_names[1] to catch CVE-2017-0199 Excel lures (test hash d30a0a6c09f664446943d82982f0630e85c447cbe84be8a74b6db6d66effbe80) where mshta.exe is started by svchost.exe running DcomLaunch, not by Office directly. A fake_services_wrong_parent rule catches services.exe with any parent other than wininit.exe (test hash fe8357febe314becf31510a7a2ecb0369e312ad58a448292f5f8a09075d7694c). The headless_console_runs_powershell rule keys on --headless in parent_name rather than requiring conhost.exe by name, catching renamed copies like rhpmx63snl.exe (which is a clean Microsoft conhost.exe dropped under a random name).
- The task_scheduler_runs_dropped_file rule closes the gap between seeing schtasks /create and knowing the task actually fired: it finds a process whose parent_name contains -s schedule or taskeng.exe, then confirms the process name contains a path that another process wrote as files_written. The dotnet_lolbin_touches_browser_logins rule is the sharpest example of three-axis correlation: it requires aspnet_compiler.exe, regasm.exe, msbuild.exe, or similar to have a scripting host anywhere in ancestor_names AND to have written paths under User Data containing Login Data, Web Data, or Cookies. On a test set of 420 malicious and 324 clean files, the ancestor_names version matched 5 malicious files the parent-only version missed and zero clean files.
Practitioner takeaway: if you maintain Livehunt rules built on vt.behaviour.processes_created, the upgrade path is to rewrite the condition as a loop over vt.behaviour.processes_list with p.parent_name or for any a in p.ancestor_names. Start by opening the Structure view of a known-bad hash in the Livehunt editor to see what the sandbox actually recorded for parent and ancestor fields before encoding assumptions. The report walks through all five rules with real hashes you can paste directly into the Livehunt tester, which works even for files analyzed before these fields were added.

item.title: An insecure neighbor: how a vulnerability chain led to an isolation bypass in cloud infrastructure
item.description:
A full tenant-isolation bypass in a major cloud provider, achieved by chaining Kubernetes escape, Konnectivity SSRF to control plane RCE, and lateral movement across a flat overlay network reaching every managed service class.
This Kaspersky SecureList report is a rare, detailed post-mortem of a successful provider-side cloud compromise found through a sanctioned bug bounty. The attacker model was a regular tenant. The outcome was total control of other tenants' clusters, databases, Redis instances, PostgreSQL clusters, and the SaltStack management plane. Every vulnerability was fixed before publication.
- The chain opened with a misconfigured managed Kubernetes cluster (k0s v1.25.16+k0s.0) that allowed privileged pod creation with hostPID. Running nsenter inside the container moved execution to the worker node host as root. From there, a Konnectivity service account token was recovered from the data-plane file system. Konnectivity's AgentService on port 8132 accepted DIAL_REQ packets from the agent without validating direction: a packet sent from the worker node caused the control-plane-side net.Dial() to connect to an arbitrary address or UNIX socket, creating a server-side request forgery primitive on the control plane. That SSRF reached /run/dbus/system_bus_socket, and through D-Bus the researchers created a transient systemd user service to run a callback binary, giving them RCE on the control plane. Mirantis confirmed the Konnectivity vulnerability. Privilege escalation to root used the OverlayFS cap_setuid capability retention bug on Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel 5.15.x.
- With root on the control plane, a flat overlay network on 100.64.0.0/10 was visible. A VictoriaMetrics instance at 100.64.13[.]37:8429 returned a full cross-tenant target list including cluster IDs and customer IDs from /api/v1/targets. VictoriaLogs on port 9428 had no authentication on its /select/logsql/query endpoint and exposed logs from all managed resources. Cloud-init scripts printed root SSH private keys to stdout, which were then stored in those shared logs. Matching VictoriaMetrics label values to VictoriaLogs records let the researchers recover private keys and tie each to the correct tenant node, enabling direct SSH access to arbitrary tenants' clusters.
- Three additional managed-service attack paths ran in parallel. Managed Kafka hosts exposed JMX Registry on port 9999 bound to the shared overlay network instead of loopback; the RMI stub-host redirect allowed loading a malicious MBean JAR via getMBeansFromURL and achieving RCE inside the Kafka JVM. Managed Redis hosts ran redis-exporter on port 9121 with a logic flaw in the /scrape handler: passing an attacker-controlled target caused the exporter to forward its own Redis AUTH credentials to that host, leaking credentials for all customer Redis instances. Managed PostgreSQL clusters running Patroni left etcd (port 2379) open without authentication; the /v2/keys/service/pg-cluster/config key stored the Patroni configuration and was writable, allowing archive_command injection; adding a standby_cluster stanza forced an immediate role conflict, Postgres restart, and archive_command execution, completing RCE on the database host. S3 backup credentials were stored on those hosts, exposing backups for all tenants.
- The SaltStack path was independent. After dumping the Salt master file system via salt-call cp.list_master and cp.get_file, the researchers found a custom pillar extension (_pillar/somebase.py) using Python string format() to build SQL queries with attacker-controlled Salt grains values, giving error-based SQL injection into the prod-cloud database. That database contained a salt-masters table with authentication tokens for every Salt master. Using those tokens against the Salt master REST API with cmd[.]run would have allowed arbitrary command execution on every minion in the cloud, covering all VDS, S3, and other managed services. The attack was stopped there by agreement with the vendor. CVE-2026-25243 affected the Valkey 7.2.11 instances: a heap overflow in RESTORE command handling via legacy hash-zipmap encoding; strict systemd sandboxing (NoExecPaths=/, CapabilityBoundingSet empty, NoNewPrivileges) was bypassed by writing a payload to /tmp and adding an SSH key to /var/lib/valkey/.ssh/authorized_keys.
Responders assessing managed cloud environments should hunt for the following evidence classes: Konnectivity or apiserver-network-proxy processes making outbound connections to UNIX sockets or unexpected internal addresses; cloud-init logs stored in centralized logging pipelines that contain private key material (search for BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY or BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY in log aggregators); etcd endpoints in managed database clusters that answer unauthenticated on port 2379 and hold service configuration keys; JMX or RMI ports bound to non-loopback addresses on managed service hosts; redis-exporter /scrape endpoints reachable from tenant networks; and Salt pillar extensions that use format() or %-style string interpolation with grain or pillar data in SQL. The full technical detail, including exploit code and command sequences, is in the Kaspersky SecureList report.

item.title: Detections Digest #20261026
item.description:
Detections Digest #20261026 roundup: 45 new rules and 50 updates across 10 repositories this week, covering PHP2Shell exploitation, AI agent abuse, BYOVD, Golden dMSA attacks, and evasive email infrastructure.
Key findings:
- PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) gets layered coverage in splunk/security_content. Zeek rules flag multipart POST requests abusing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS to inject serialized PHP objects or PHP tags in filename headers. Splunk correlates Apache and Nginx logs for memory exhaustion faults and POST bodies 1MB or larger returning HTTP 500. A separate process rule catches inline PHP execution via -r, --run, and -s switches across standard interpreters, phpdbg, and FrankenPHP without a file being written to disk. Parent process coverage for webshell spawning rules also now includes caddy, frankenphp, roadrunner, lighttpd, and iisexpress.
- SigmaHQ/sigma adds end-to-end Defendnot coverage, targeting a hacktool that disables Windows Defender through undocumented Windows Security Center APIs. Detections span PowerShell download cradles, binary execution by import hash, registry tampering against Security Center AV provider keys, and scheduled task creation via Event IDs 4698 and 4702. Golden dMSA attack detection covers Event ID 4662 reads on msDS-DelegatedManagedServiceAccount and msKds-ProvRootKey objects, Event ID 4771 Kerberos pre-auth failures with codes 0x18 and 0x19 on machine accounts, and GoldenDMSA tool execution by command-line pattern. LSASS access rules drop the SYNCHRONIZE mask (0x100000) to cut EDR-generated noise while keeping credential dumping visibility.
- AI agent and LLM threat rules expand significantly. Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules adds detection for zero-width, soft-hyphen, and bidirectional Unicode control characters in MCP tool descriptions and SKILL[.]md files, mapped to MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051.001. SSRF logic now covers apex loopback wildcard domains, IPv4-mapped IPv6 subnets, internal-only domains (.internal, .local, .lan), and non-HTTP protocols including file, gopher, dict, ldap, and tftp. CVEs tracked across these rules include CVE-2025-68143, CVE-2025-68144, CVE-2026-0628, CVE-2026-55096, CVE-2019-5418, and CVE-2021-21311. Sublime-security adds prompt injection rules for calendar invites (.ics), invisible HTML Unicode sequences, and plain email bodies.
- LOLRMM adds Sigma coverage for Ping32 (registry, process, network to cloud.nsecsoft[.]com, and file artifacts) and rogue VS Code Remote Tunnels with code-insiders.exe placed under C:\Windows\debug and outbound connections to global.rel.tunnels.api.visualstudio[.]com. LOLDrivers refreshes MD5, SHA1, SHA256, and IMPHASH lists for BYOVD rules covering both malicious and vulnerable driver loads, including environments with HVCI enabled.
- The digest's engineering tip is worth operationalizing: defanged literals copied from threat reports into live query strings fail silently because they never match raw telemetry. The RuleCheck checks Q0700, Q0710-Q0713, Q0721, and Q0722 codify validation for IP and CIDR syntax, cloud IP overlap across AWS, Azure, GCP, and Cloudflare, hash format, and defanged value detection. If your team maintains an internal detection repository, run these checks before your next rule deployment, and audit existing rules for the SYNCHRONIZE mask noise pattern the LSASS updates address this week.

- The digest's engineering tip is worth operationalizing: defanged literals copied from threat reports into live query strings fail silently because they never match raw telemetry. item.title: PHP2Shell Weaponized After Japanese Real Estate Extortion
item.description:
Extortion operator "kkkkevin777" exposed their full staging server, revealing a shared-hosting pivot across nearly 20 Japanese 🇯🇵 real estate sites, 16,061 plaintext member records, and a weaponized PHP2Shell toolkit staged for what comes next.
Key findings:
- An open HTTP directory listing on 96.126.130[.]81 port 9999 exposed the operator's entire working environment: web shells, beacon and C2 logs, ransom page templates, SSH private keys, stolen databases, and a weaponized copy of the PHP2Shell reproducer package for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (unauthenticated memory corruption in PHP session upload progress handling). File timestamps place the bulk of activity between October 8 and October 27, 2026, with the PHP2Shell tooling arriving October 21, roughly ten days after the extortion wave. No saved output on the server confirms a successful PHP2Shell exploitation of a live target, but the tooling was staged and follow-on probe scripts were ready.
- Initial access to one Japanese 🇯🇵 real estate services company was already held by October 9. The operator placed PHP web shells with random 32-character hexadecimal names under image upload directories (artifact: .whk.php in the web root), injected a beacon into the site's database config calling back to 96.126.130[.]81:9001 via /b?h=hostname, and installed a cron job rewriting .htaccess to "Require all granted" every minute (T1053.003) to undo the owner's lockout attempts. MITRE coverage includes T1190, T1505.003, T1071.001, T1491.002, and T1490.
- A single SSH private key stored on the staging server (key comment: administrator@chenzicccc) and one database password reused across victim sites turned one compromise into beacon callbacks from roughly 20 Japanese 🇯🇵 domains between October 9 and 11 (T1552.004, T1021.004). The operator also swept victims' home directories for backup files to limit recovery options, and on October 22 and 23 pivoted to a Taiwanese 🇹🇼 Windows server, pulling five SQL Server database backups, 663 FoxPro files, and 730 business emails via web shell.
- The stolen haul on the server includes 16,061 member records from the initial victim with plaintext passwords, annual income, savings, occupation, and property search details. A bulk-mail script was staged to send each member their own data plus 49 other members' records from the victim's own mail server, and a draft 5ch newsplus post accused the company of failing to notify Japan's 🇯🇵 Personal Information Protection Commission. Email addresses in the stolen data touch major Japanese 🇯🇵 banking, telecom, and technology consumer mail domains, creating downstream phishing and credential-stuffing exposure well beyond the breached sites.
- The operator's scripts carry Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 comments, every victim-facing message is written in Japanese 🇯🇵, the ransom contact is kkkkevin777@tutamail[.]com with a fallback at theudinhthi421@gmail[.]com, and a separate Python C2 on port 8443 paired with a PowerShell agent (T1059.001) was labeled a "finance line" beacon for operations outside the real estate campaign. On October 21, the same day PHP2Shell arrived, the operator compiled 3,913 Hong Kong and Taiwanese 🇹🇼 IP ranges and ran mass scans against them.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt web roots for the string 96.126.130[.]81, for .whk.php, for files matching *.orig20261010, and for PHP files with 32-character hexadecimal names in upload or image directories. Review every hosting account's crontab for entries rewriting .htaccess, audit authorized_keys for the administrator@chenzicccc comment, and check web server logs for multipart requests with unusually long filenames returning HTTP 500, a pattern the report associates with PHP2Shell exploitation attempts. On shared hosting, audit every other account's SSH authorized_keys and database passwords if any co-tenant was touched: one reused credential was the entire pivot mechanism here. IOCs, beacon URI patterns, file artifacts, and the full MITRE mapping are in the SOCRadar report.

item.title: Private repos still leak secrets to Gheist, a stolen GitHub token campaign
item.description:
A GitHub Actions campaign called Gheist has harvested secrets from private repositories across 850+ compromised accounts by exploiting a gap in GitHub's workflow approval protections that only covers public repos.
Key findings:
- Gheist operates with a stolen GitHub token and no external attacker infrastructure. The tool enumerates every repository the token can reach, creates a branch named ci-sync- plus six random characters, commits a workflow file called sync-check, triggers it automatically on push, and exfiltrates secrets through GitHub's own API. The run log is deleted seconds after download, leaving a narrow evidence window. Because exfil travels entirely over GitHub's API, there is no outbound domain or C2 connection to block at the network layer.
- GitHub's secret masking is bypassed by Base32-encoding each secret before printing it to the workflow run log. GitHub only redacts a secret that appears exactly as stored, so the encoded output prints in full and is downloaded via API. Wiz recovered more than 13,500 planted branches across the 850+ accounts, which gives a sense of scale before deletion.
- The critical protection gap: GitHub's July 28 hold on potentially malicious workflow runs applies only to public repositories. Private repositories and GitHub Enterprise Server are unprotected. Wiz confirmed exploitation by cross-referencing GitHub audit logs showing ci-sync-* branch runs completing and then being deleted by the gheist user agent, and CloudTrail showing those branches triggering Actions that assumed AWS roles, proving execution happened without any approval gate.
- In at least one enterprise intrusion, the tool cycled through tokens for multiple users and automation accounts within minutes, cloned private repositories, and hours later cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager. One Gheist variant added a second job on October 19 that targets self-hosted runners, searching the host for tokens and keys and using Docker to reach host filesystem contents.
- The same compromised accounts are shared infrastructure. On October 6, 391 accounts renamed roughly 1,461 repositories to cracked-software lures. On October 18, 25 Gheist accounts each created a "Windows RDP Runner" repository within a nine-minute window. This overlap means a single account compromise may serve multiple campaigns simultaneously.
DFIR takeaway: If your workflows use OIDC to authenticate to cloud providers, query your CloudTrail or equivalent cloud audit log for role assumption events whose subject field contains a ci-sync- branch name. That evidence survives even if you have no GitHub log retention. In GitHub audit logs, filter for the gheist user agent. Deleted runs and branches do not undo the secret exposure: rotate every repository, organization, and environment secret accessible to any affected repository, and revoke the tokens that pushed the commits.

item.title: The Blind Spot You Created on Purpose. The Real Architecture of Microsoft Defender Exclusions
item.description:
Microsoft Defender exclusions are not a master key: they are engine-specific bypasses with cross-platform behavior differences that can silently kill EDR visibility, and attackers know how to exploit that.
Key findings:
- Defender is not a single engine. It is composed of Antivirus, Attack Surface Reduction, Controlled Folder Access, Network Protection, and automated remediation, each with its own exclusion surface. Adding a path exclusion to silence a false positive does not mean all engines stop watching. On Windows, EDR telemetry and behavioral alerting continue inside excluded folders. On macOS, exclusions are antivirus-only with EDR still active. On Linux, the distinction is critical: standard Antivirus Exclusions skip file scanning but preserve process telemetry, while Global Exclusions operate at the fanotify/eBPF kernel sensor level and blind both AV and EDR alert generation simultaneously.
- The priority chain on Windows is the source of the most dangerous misconception in the report's opening scenario. Defender evaluates rules in a fixed order and stops at the first match: Application Control (WDAC/AppLocker) first, then Antivirus Exclusions, then custom Indicators. An active Antivirus path exclusion for C:\Builds causes Defender to grant an immediate scan bypass before it ever evaluates a Block IoC for a known malicious hash. A SOC-created block indicator on a file hash is effectively dead on a machine where the file lives in an excluded path.
- Process exclusions carry hidden blast radius. Excluding a named process does not limit the impact to file scanning. On Windows, a process exclusion can also suppress Network Protection inspection of that process's outbound connections, meaning attacker C2 traffic originating from a compromised or injected excluded process passes uninspected. The report flags code injection into an excluded process as the key threat vector here.
- Conflicting indicators follow a documented tiebreaker order: SHA-256 beats SHA-1 beats MD5; device-group-scoped indicators beat organization-wide ones; full URLs beat domain-level indicators. An Allow indicator for a hash or certificate grants execution before ASR rules, CFA, or heuristic scans can act on the behavior.
Takeaway: Hunt your own exclusion configuration before an attacker does. The report includes two KQL queries for Advanced Hunting you can deploy now. The first queries DeviceRegistryEvents for RegistryValueSet actions where RegistryKey contains "Windows Defender\Exclusions" and DeviceProcessEvents for PowerShell (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, powershell_ise.exe) running Add-MpPreference or Set-MpPreference with "Exclusion" in the command line, both with a 7-day lookback. The second uses a baseline/recent-window comparison against DeviceProcessEvents scoped to your known excluded folder paths, surfacing any SHA256 hashes that executed in the last 7 days but were not seen in the prior 14-day baseline. On Linux, audit whether any Global Exclusions exist at all: that setting should require explicit sign-off because it removes both scanning and EDR coverage simultaneously.

item.title: Attackers Hijack Dahua IP Cameras in Ukraine Using P2P Access and Auth Weaknesses
item.description:
Dahua IP cameras in Ukraine 🇺🇦 are being hijacked at scale via predictable serial numbers, auth bypass CVEs, and P2P cloud relay abuse, with Russian 🇷🇺 actors using the footage for real-time military intelligence.
Key findings:
- The core attack surface is Easy4IP, Dahua's P2P cloud platform. Serial numbers follow a predictable structure: a 10-character model prefix shared across an entire device family, plus a 5-character sequential hex counter (e.g., 7K01F36PCA003E8). Attackers brute-force these at scale with no rate limiting or lockout, then reach cameras through Dahua's own cloud relay even when the device sits behind a NAT with no direct internet exposure. 283 cameras in Operation CameraSwarm were accessed by serial number alone through the cloud relay, with no device address and in many cases no credentials at all.
- Authentication barriers fall through two routes: weak or default passwords and exploitation of CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045, authentication bypass flaws in outdated Dahua firmware that allow passwordless login. Operation CameraSwarm (June 17 to July 22, 2026) combined credential brute-force against TCP port 37777 (Dahua's default DVRIP management and streaming port) with this CVE chain, compromising over 14,530 cameras. A related Russian-speaking campaign used Ingram, a public webcam vulnerability scanner, to exploit those same Dahua CVEs alongside CVE-2017-7921 and CVE-2021-36260 in Hikvision, CVE-2020-25078 in D-Link, and CVE-2020-25169 in Reolink, compromising 58 devices and extending scanning to TP-Link and MikroTik routers across 15 European countries using CVE-2024-53375 and CVE-2024-57049.
- The most forensically significant artifact from Operation CameraSwarm is a persistent backdoor account with credentials p2pwn / p2password, installed over RPC after either bypass method. It is stored independently of the admin password and survives both a password change and, on most firmware, a factory reset. 1,923 cameras carry this account. This means remediation that stops at a password reset or factory reset is incomplete on affected firmware versions.
- CERT-UA identifies three on-device indicators: presence of unknown accounts, unauthorized configuration changes, and audit log entries showing authentication events using DVRIP from 127.0.0.1, which is the signature of P2P relay access rather than a direct inbound connection. That local-address auth event is the key log artifact distinguishing cloud-relay compromise from conventional remote access.
- Dutch 🇳🇱 intelligence assessed in July 2026 that Russian 🇷🇺 actors are running automated image recognition against compromised camera feeds to identify military vehicles, track EU and NATO weapons deliveries to Ukraine 🇺🇦, locate Ukrainian 🇺🇦 military personnel, and correlate transport routes. The camera compromise is not opportunistic surveillance; it feeds a targeting and logistics intelligence pipeline.
Practitioner takeaway: On any Dahua device in scope, pull the audit log and filter for DVRIP authentication events sourced from 127.0.0.1. That pattern is CERT-UA's indicator of P2P relay access and should be treated as evidence of unauthorized entry even if no external IP is present. Enumerate all accounts and compare against known-good baselines; the p2pwn account persists through factory reset on most firmware, so account enumeration after reset is still required. Disable Easy4IP P2P if the feature is not operationally required, and apply firmware updates to address CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045. IOCs and campaign detail are in the Hunt[.]io report on Operation CameraSwarm.

item.title: How to Export Kubernetes Audit Logs
item.description:
Kubernetes audit logs are the forensic record of every API call to your cluster, but they are off by default on self-managed clusters and EKS, meaning an incident in an unmonitored cluster leaves responders with nothing to work from.
Key details:
- Where the log lives depends entirely on who runs your control plane. Self-managed clusters write JSON-lines to the path set by the audit-log-path flag, typically /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log, confirmed via /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. EKS sends to CloudWatch Logs under the /aws/eks/[cluster]/cluster log group with the kube-audit-admin stream prefix. AKS writes to a Log Analytics workspace in the AKSAuditAdmin table (note: this table excludes get and list calls, meaning secret reads are invisible unless you switch to the kube-audit category). GKE enables Admin Activity audit logging by default, but Data Access logging for Kubernetes is opt-in.
- The audit policy level determines what evidence survives. Metadata level records who acted on which object and when, but not the request body. Request or RequestResponse level captures the full payload, so you can see whether a pod spec requested privileged: true or a hostPath mount. If you do not know which level was active during the incident window, your evidence is potentially incomplete.
- The API calls that matter most in an investigation: create on pods/exec (objectRef.subresource: exec) shows someone opened a shell in a running container. create of a ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin is a privilege escalation to full cluster control. get or list on secrets by an unusual identity indicates credential harvesting. Pods created with privileged, hostPath, or hostNetwork set a path to node escape. user.username: system:anonymous with a 2xx response confirms anonymous access succeeded. Bursts of 403s from a single service account suggest a stolen token probing its permissions.
- Rotated audit files on self-managed clusters carry a timestamp in the filename and sit alongside the active log. If your incident window extends beyond the current file, those rotated files must be collected too or the timeline has gaps.
Takeaway: Before pulling logs, confirm audit logging was actually enabled for the incident window. On self-managed clusters, check /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml for both audit-policy-file and audit-log-path. On EKS, verify the audit log type is enabled under Cluster, Observability, control plane logging. On AKS, check Diagnostic settings for the kube-audit or kube-audit-admin category. If logging was off, you have no historical data and your focus shifts to enabling it and preserving whatever runtime state remains. The report includes platform-specific CLI commands using aws logs filter-log-events, az monitor log-analytics query, and gcloud logging read with timestamp-bounded queries to scope the export to your incident window.

item.title: Kernel eviction notice: What wesp.sys reveals about the Windows Endpoint Security Platform
item.description:
Microsoft's Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP) reverse-engineered from Insider build binaries: a single Microsoft-owned kernel driver aims to replace every vendor's EDR kernel component, but key blocking capability is not yet present.
Key findings:
- wesp.sys lives in System32\Drivers and registers as a file system mini-filter at altitude 329500, sitting above WdFilter (328010) in the filter stack. It carries public symbols on the Microsoft symbol server, so a local kernel debugging session in WinDbg exposes its internals without source. The companion user-mode library espclient.dll lives in System32 and exports a C-based API where every function is prefixed Esp, covering rules and filter configuration. These two binaries are the entire public surface of WESP right now.
- Communication between wesp.sys and user-mode clients runs through a FilterCommunicationPort object named ESPFilterPort, visible in WinObj under the root object manager directory. The driver has no device objects and handles no IRP major functions itself, so DeviceIoControl is off the table entirely. espclient.dll imports FilterConnectCommunicationPort, FilterGetMessage, and FilterSendMessage from FltLib.dll, but notably not FilterReplyMessage. That omission matters: without reply capability, user-mode clients cannot send a blocking decision back to the driver, meaning process creation veto is not yet implemented.
- The motivation is the July 2024 CrowdStrike outage, where a bad content update crashed 8.5 million machines by faulting the vendor's kernel driver. WESP consolidates the kernel footprint into one Microsoft-tested driver, replacing the current model where every EDR ships its own kernel component. Notifications for process, thread, image, handle, registry, file system, and network events would all route through wesp.sys, though coverage today is partial and undocumented.
- Filtering at the source is architecturally central: the Esp-prefixed exports confirm rule and filter objects exist in the client API, designed to drop high-volume events (registry reads, file reads) inside the driver before they ever reach user mode. This is essential for performance given the volume ProcMon illustrates at idle. Client processes must run elevated and will likely require Protected Process Light (PPL) status signed by Microsoft.
Practitioner takeaway: For defenders and researchers, run fltmc in an elevated prompt on Insider builds and confirm wesp at altitude 329500. Enumerate ESPFilterPort in WinObj to verify the communication channel is active. The absence of FilterReplyMessage in espclient.dll is the key gap to track: until that or an equivalent is present, WESP cannot support inline blocking, and EDR vendors will need to retain their own kernel drivers for enforcement capability. Watch Microsoft's symbol server and Insider changelogs for updates to both binaries as the capability matures.

item.title: Researchers Uncover Rentable Android Spyware uCreater Targeting WeChat and Telegram
item.description:
Rentable Android spyware platform uCreater embeds inside repackaged Telegram, WeChat, and GCash apps to steal credentials, OTPs, and wallet data through a multi-tenant operator model active since at least 2021.
Key details:
- uCreater uses app virtualization (VirtualApp, LSPatch, Pine) to run malicious code inside legitimate, signed applications without requiring root. LSPatch stores the original APK at cache/lspatch/origin/*.apk and loads hooks from an asset named TgJarPine.dex. These two paths are your primary on-device artifact. The presence of either strongly suggests a repackaged, instrumented app.
- The Telegram module's Db_MessagesStorageRawQuery handler accepts operator-supplied SQL and runs it directly against the live app database, reaching encrypted or locally stored message data while the app is running. A separate hook on Telegram's SRPHelper.getX routine captures the two-step verification password in cleartext before hashing. Operators can also list or delete sessions, change the linked phone number, and remove their own session from the victim's device list to conceal access.
- Post-installation instrumentation is retrieved from Alibaba OSS and MinIO buckets and paths named Huuk_<target> and fengzhuang-app. The distribution domain telegram-apk.uzyzx[.]com was identified as a delivery host. The control server's address is pulled from Redis using the Domain key, with signed JSON beacons reporting to endpoints matching /api/callback/Tg*. Five samples confirmed active contact with the control server, targeting Telegram, Telegram-X, and WeChat.
- Infrastructure recovered from an exposed GitLab server includes Spring Cloud services for command dispatch, authorization capture, data collection, and message bridging, plus a Vue admin console. Roughly three dozen developers are identified in commit histories, with timestamps consistent with China 🇨🇳 time and at least one corporate email tied to Tanzhou, a Changsha software firm. The control server holds ICP filing 湘ICP备2024061212号, and a Censys search on the operator's Tengine gateway fingerprint returned roughly 48 hosts. Three companies are linked to the platform: Hunan Youchuang Technology (ucreater[.]com, videoflow[.]cn), Changsha Sukai Network (qianxuncc[.]cn), and Changsha Zhuoqing E-commerce (uip.exe signing identity).
- The WeChat module's _2_0_UploadAppLoginInfo command retrieves login identity and packages app data for upload to OSS, supporting account cloning. The bundled Pine engine fails on Android 17 due to API changes, but the July 2026 sample still ships the outdated engine, meaning Pixel 10 Pro with Android 17 currently resists that component while other devices remain untested.
Practitioner takeaway: on a suspicious Android device, look for cache/lspatch/origin/*.apk and the TgJarPine.dex asset as primary indicators of LSPatch-based repackaging. Check installed APK signing certificates against the known-good originals for Telegram, Telegram-X, WeChat, and GCash. For network visibility, watch for callbacks to /api/callback/Tg* endpoints and outbound connections to Alibaba OSS or MinIO from messaging app processes. The report contains no IOC table or detection rules, but the infrastructure details above are drawn directly from the researcher's findings.

item.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
item.description:
KV cache tenant isolation failure in Cloudflare's GLM-5.3 Workers AI model leaked other users' prompt and generation data across 155 responses over 13 days before coordinated remediation with SGLang.
Key findings:
- The exposure ran from August 27 to September 9, 2026, affecting only the [@]cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 model. Any prompt exceeding 681,280 tokens could receive a response that included KV cache pages written by a prior user's request. In total 155 responses were confirmed affected. Cloudflare found no evidence of deliberate exploitation: timing and volume were consistent with ordinary long-context use, not repeated probing.
- Two overlapping conditions caused the leak. The prefill KV pool was sized at 681,280 tokens while the advertised context window was 1,048,576 tokens. SGLang's rejection path for over-length requests swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder but did not abort the disaggregated handoff: the decode node received a "transfer complete" signal, assumed full prefill had occurred, and attended over stale pages from earlier requests. The client got HTTP 200, a coherent reply, and content belonging to other sessions.
- The forensic signature is subtle. Affected responses arrived faster than a full 8-page prefill should take, prompt_tokens matched the long prompt, and output was coherent but drawn from prior tenants' cached state. Any operator running SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode with a KV pool smaller than the configured context length is in the same exposure class. The fix for this specific failure path is in SGLang PR #36988 (v0.5.20) and #38935 (v0.5.21), with the full hardened release in v0.5.22.
- Cloudflare's response took roughly 40 minutes from incident declaration to the model going offline (declared at 13:22 UTC, offline by 14:00 UTC on September 9). The corrected configuration, which aligned pool size to exceed context length at roughly 2.04 million tokens, was deployed by 14:52 UTC. A Cloudflare-authored engine patch that correctly retires rejected requests before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer was validated against the researcher's reproduction script and the model restored by 19:40 UTC.
- A broader class of KV cache memory-safety bugs in SGLang disaggregated deployments is now documented. Issues include page lifetime races within a single decode node and cross-node races where an aborted request's RDMA writes land in a new request's pages after the pages are freed. Cloudflare has contributed upstream patches and a reproduction script across PRs including #30899, #38961, #32758, and #39500, which adds a per-transfer KV checksum via --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum.
Operator action: if you run SGLang in disaggregated mode, pull the KV pool size from the engine's startup log and compare it directly to your configured context length after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. Do not infer safety from HTTP response codes alone. Upgrade to SGLang v0.5.22 or later to get both the admission fix and the deferred KV release defaults. Enable --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary where your model architecture supports them, and check logs to confirm requests are being verified. The Cloudflare Security report contains the full timeline, upstream PR list, and operator checklist.

item.title: Magento Campaign Infects 953 Online Stores Across Five Domains
item.description:
A skimmer group has quietly infected 953 Magento stores across 15 months, rotating through five loader domains and now deploying browser fingerprinting to defeat automated scanners before delivering the final payload.
Key details:
- The campaign, tracked by Sansec as PolyShell mass attack since July 2025, uses five loader domains: manulfie[.]click (863 stores), neswnsssn[.]click (494), lanhd6549tdhse[.]top (355), additionalver[.]com (246), and the newest, deepveindrilling[.]com (83 stores, registered October 6, 2026). Two additional domains, hdfdsi84j3h[.]top and c85grt98sd[.]com, appeared on smaller subsets. The group rotates domains every few months and has re-registered expired ones through a parking service, meaning expired domains can still execute attacker-controlled scripts in visitor browsers.
- The loader lives exclusively in Magento's cms_block table, not in core_config_data or theme files. Sansec found it across 148 server installs over the campaign. The October rewrite replaced a plain script tag with an inline loader that sends a browser fingerprint to hxxps://deepveindrilling[.]com/?s=49b7ca5f&fp=, probing navigator.webdriver, Selenium globals, ChromeDriver's cdc_ properties, WebGL GPU name, CPU cores, memory, screen size, time zone, languages, and client hints before deciding whether to serve a payload. When urlscan[.]io hit an infected store with an automated Chrome browser, it got a clean HTTP 200 with no injected content: the filter works.
- The persistence mechanism changed from the March version. The loader sets a value called fpCode in the visitor's browser storage. On every subsequent page view, a second script reads fpCode, drops the stored code into a hidden div, and triggers it as a click event handler, bypassing eval() entirely. The payload re-executes on every visit even if deepveindrilling[.]com goes offline or gets blocked. Older payloads tied to earlier domains loaded scripts from leqdger[.]click (a Ledger wallet typosquat) and routed real visitors through Keitaro, a commercial traffic distribution system, at hxxps://additionalver[.]com/Mb2z8J?&se_referrer= before serving skimmer code.
- Initial access came through file upload vulnerabilities, specifically CVE-2026-48356 (PolyShell, patched by Adobe as APSB26-73) and CVE-2025-54236 (SessionReaper, patched as APSB25-88). In March the group injected into 471 stores in a single hour using PolyShell webshells, some disguised as PNG images. One store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 with all core patches applied was still infected on October 23, with a rogue admin account and a GSocket backdoor already present, confirming that unpatched entry is not the only path.
Practitioner takeaway: Query your Magento database cms_block and cms_page tables for the strings fpCode and se_referrer and check for base64-encoded domain strings. Hunt uploaded files for webshells, including those with image extensions. Enumerate admin accounts for unknowns and check for GSocket or other backdoor processes. Removing the script alone is not remediation: the write access that placed it remains until the original vulnerability or backdoor is closed. After cleanup, rotate database, admin, and API credentials. IOCs are listed at the end of Sansec's report.

Practitioner takeaway: Query your Magento database cms_block and cms_page tables for the strings fpCode and se_referrer and check for base64-encoded domain strings. Hunt uploaded files for webshells, including those with image extensions. Enumerate admin accounts for unknowns and check for GSocket or other backdoor processes. Removing the script alone is not remediation: the write access that placed it remains until the original vulnerability or backdoor is closed. After cleanup, rotate database, admin, and API credentials. IOCs are listed at the end of Sansec's report.

item.title: How Criminals Abuse Claude’s Own Website to Spread Malware
item.description:
Attackers weaponized Anthropic's own claude[.]ai domain to distribute AMOS infostealer and a Windows RAT via ClickFix lures, backed by paid Google Ads pointing at pages that carry every trust signal a user would check.
Key findings:
- The lure pages are real claude[.]ai URLs, served as Shared Chats (claude[.]ai/share/...) and public Artifacts (claude[.]ai/artifact/...), neither of which required compromising Anthropic's infrastructure. The only warning is a thin "Content is user-generated and unverified" banner. The domain, padlock, and Claude branding are all genuine. Links recovered by Gen Threat Labs carry Google Ads tracking parameters (gclid, gad_campaignid), confirming a funded malvertising operation with multiple rotating Artifacts tied to two separate ad campaigns.
- The macOS chain is a ClickFix attack: the fake "Install on macOS" Artifact walks the victim through opening Terminal, copying an obfuscated one-liner, and pressing Enter. The clipboard payload hides the attacker's server address inside an encoded blob. A loader script fetches a second script, which pulls the final AppleScript-based payload from the Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS) family. If AMOS lacks Full Disk Access it writes a persistence line to the shell startup file and waits. Once access is granted it presents a fake System Preferences password prompt, harvests Keychain data, browser credentials and session cookies from Chromium and Gecko-based browsers, crypto wallet files, and documents with extensions including .pdf, .docx, .key, .seed, .pem, .wallet, and .ovpn, then exfiltrates everything as a ZIP to the attacker's server and deletes its temp files.
- When AMOS detects Ledger Live, Ledger Wallet, or Trezor Suite it downloads a trojanized replacement from the attacker and overwrites the legitimate binary. On next launch the fake app prompts the victim to "restore" or "validate" their recovery phrase, including a fake progress animation for Trezor. The typed phrase is sent to a second, separate attacker-controlled domain built solely to collect seed phrases. Seed phrase compromise means total, irreversible loss of every derived wallet.
- The Windows campaign uses an Artifact titled "Install Claude on Windows," also pushed via paid ads. The ClickFix variant instructs Win + R, Ctrl + V, Enter to execute a PowerShell command that prints fake "Challenge in progress" progress messages to appear benign, then reaches out to a github.io-hosted second stage carrying an encrypted .NET payload. The final payload injects into a legitimate Windows process to hide from the task list, enumerates installed antivirus, takes desktop screenshots, reads active window titles, and maintains a persistent connection to an attacker C2, behaving as a remote-access tool with operator control rather than a run-once stealer. It also hunts desktop crypto wallets including Electrum, Exodus, Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Ledger, plus browser-based wallet extensions.
DFIR takeaway: On macOS, triage the shell startup files (~/.zshrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.zprofile) for injected persistence lines added by AMOS, and check for unexpected Full Disk Access grants in System Settings. Look for a recently created ZIP in or near the user's temp directories before deletion, and examine Keychain access logs for bulk reads by a process that is not a known browser or system binary. On Windows, hunt for PowerShell spawned from explorer.exe or the Run dialog with no parent script path, followed by outbound connections to github[.]io and an unknown C2. Process injection into benign Windows processes paired with screenshot activity and a long-lived outbound socket are the behavioral signature of the RAT stage. For any suspected compromise: assume full credential theft, rotate email and exchange credentials from a clean device, revoke sessions, and treat any crypto wallet whose seed may have been typed into an unexpected prompt as fully drained. IOCs and campaign details are in the Gen Threat Labs report.

item.title: AI, Scripts, Operator: Inside the ConnectWise Attack
item.description:
Storm-0940 abused compromised ConnectWise cloud backup credentials to hit more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, reaching Global Administrator in under three hours, with behavioral evidence pointing to an AI agent adapting the tooling mid-operation.
Key findings:
- The attack chain ran in three modes on October 15: scripted loops fired token requests against nearly 1,000 tenants in ascending tenant ID order using Python-urllib/3.12 from 144.172.64[.]128, a thread pool burst 100 requests in under 10 seconds at 13 to 21 attempts per second, and a pilot-then-batch pattern tested actions in one tenant before batching them, a sequence observed three times across two tools. The password spray phase, October 10 to 14, originated from 144.172.64[.]99 and 194.165.16[.]21. Entry came via compromised ConnectWise application credentials (T1078.004, T1199), bypassing any per-user authentication entirely.
- The strongest behavioral signal for an agent in the loop came at 03:48:24 UTC: a certificate upload failed on a thumbprint mismatch with no retry. Fifty-five seconds later the next run added exponential backoff retry logic (3.5 seconds, then 7.1 seconds) that had not existed before, and carried it into a second tenant 47 seconds after that. A script does not rewrite itself between runs. Huntress rates LLM involvement at low-to-medium on their telemetry alone, rising to medium-to-high when Microsoft's attribution to Storm-0940 using ARTEX (T1588.007) is factored in. ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent framework that builds an asset graph and runs parallel breach paths from recon through exfiltration with minimal human interaction.
- Privilege escalation (T1098.003) used the Teams service principal to assign itself Global Administrator via Microsoft Graph, then granted elevated roles to sibling service principals when a removal failed. Credential persistence (T1098.001) involved adding secrets and uploading certificates to victim application identities. A critical visibility gap: Microsoft Graph reads are not recorded in Entra audit logs, and no known victim had Graph activity logging enabled, so the full scope of data access cannot be reconstructed from available logs. Application-only audit events also carry no source IP, making some credential changes untraceable to a specific address.
- The operation was clumsy but effective: secrets were added and removed and added again, a certificate failed, and single-tenant app secrets were replayed against a hundred tenants where they could never work. Despite that, the stolen application credential compressed the attack from targeting to privileged access across multiple environments in under three hours. The user agent strings show deliberate manipulation (T1036): python-requests/2.31 instead of the library default python-requests/2.31.0, and a browser string missing its standard "(KHTML, like Gecko)" segment, both consistent with a model generating strings from memory rather than copying them from a live library.
Practitioner takeaway: The detections that held here will not hold long. Cadence and retry timing were the most useful signals in this investigation, and a better tool will normalize them away. Focus on what the activity does, not how it looks. Alert on any service principal assigning itself Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator (T1098.003), credential additions to high-privilege applications from unexpected sources (T1098.001), and any vendor application deviating from its baseline user agent, the clearest early signal was kiota-dotnet being replaced by Python-urllib/3.12. Enable Microsoft Graph activity logs now where licensing allows, and preserve raw user agent strings and sub-second timestamps because normalization destroys the signals. Watch estate-wide: what looks like a trickle per tenant is thousands of attempts per minute across the whole estate. IOCs including 144.172.64[.]128, 144.172.64[.]99, 144.172.64[.]60, 194.165.16[.]21, and full MITRE ATT&CK mappings are in the Huntress report.

item.title: Attackers Use Microsoft Teams IT Support Scams to Deploy Malware and Ransomware
item.description:
Microsoft Teams external chat is the new phishing lure: hundreds of cases share the same IT-impersonation playbook, ending in RMM abuse, backdoor deployment, and Chaos ransomware.
Key findings:
- The attack chain opens with mail bombing, flooding the target inbox with newsletter confirmations to manufacture urgency, then a Teams message arrives from an external tenant using IT-themed display names like "IT Support (Internal)", "HelpDesk Supervisor", or "Enterprise IT & Security (Internal)". Attackers now add the victim organization's own domain or company name to the display name to defeat the external-user warning banner. Between 30-40% of cases use *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant names such as helpdeskteam365.onmicrosoft[.]com, itendpoint365.onmicrosoft[.]com, itcoreportal.onmicrosoft[.]com, and itadmin922.onmicrosoft[.]com. Roughly 50% of paid-TLD variants use .top, consistent with STAC4749 tradecraft previously linked to Chaos ransomware by Sophos.
- Once the victim engages, vishing moves them to grant remote hands-on-keyboard access via legitimate RMM tools: Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, or LogMeIn. The remote session is then used to navigate directly to payload URLs, deliberately bypassing Safe Links and ZAP scanning by avoiding pasting URLs into Teams chat itself.
- In documented cases, the attacker instructs the user to run a PowerShell command that pulls an MSI installer from Microsoft Azure Blob Storage. That installer launches a PowerShell script which extracts and executes a Python implant. The implant then runs a second MSI transaction issuing LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects and exfiltrates the results externally. A second payload, the GoGRPC backdoor, has also been observed alongside the RMM tool Level deployed for redundant access before lateral movement to domain controllers and final ransomware staging.
- Attackers deliberately avoid pasting URLs into Teams to evade message-scanning controls, instead navigating to payloads themselves during the remote session. Arctic Wolf notes that endpoint and identity telemetry are the essential monitoring surfaces here, not message scanning alone. Microsoft's built-in Notes feature within Teams has also been observed as a delivery mechanism for attacker content in a subset of cases.
Practitioner takeaway: prioritize endpoint and identity telemetry over message-scanning for this vector. Hunt for RMM tool installations (Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Level) preceded by Teams external chat activity in your collaboration logs, then pivot to PowerShell spawning msiexec with arguments pointing to Azure Blob Storage URLs. Review Entra ID / Azure AD sign-in logs for newly created external tenants with .onmicrosoft[.]com or .top domains initiating chat sessions. If your organization does not require external Teams chat, disable it at the tenant level. IOCs and infrastructure patterns are detailed in the Arctic Wolf Labs report.

item.title: Looking for a Language [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 21st)
item.description:
HTTP Accept-Language and Accept-Charset headers in web honeypot logs expose automated scanning campaigns, including hosts in Canadian 🇨🇦 AS space broadcasting Mainland Chinese 🇨🇳 character set preferences while probing internet-facing endpoints.
Key findings:
- A DShield SIEM honeypot on a Raspberry Pi collected roughly 960,000 log records across just over 3 weeks, yet only 15,271 triggered any detection rule. The remaining 944,000-plus records went unruled, which is exactly the gap this analysis targets. The method is iterative feature selection: use Kibana Field Statistics to find fields with low distinct-value counts (Distribution 2 to 6), eliminate fields that are uniform across all records, and home in on the outlier values that demand explanation.
- The pivot started with the http.request.mime_type field, where a subset of records sent the Accept-Charset value "GBK,utf-8;q=0.7,*;q=0.3". GBK is the Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 character set extension of GB 2312. Finding that preference explicitly declared in requests hitting a non-Chinese honeypot was the first anomaly. Filtering on that exact string narrowed 960,000 records to 47.
- Geolocation on those 47 records showed two source regions: Beijing (expected) and Ontario (not expected). The Ontario traffic traced to AS-7456. Pivoting on that autonomous system number and running the same distribution analysis revealed that all 31 records with an explicit Accept-Language header declared zh-CN as their primary language preference, either "zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.6" or "zh-CN,zh;q=0.8". No attempt was made to suppress or rotate these headers.
- The 6 source IPs tied to AS-7456 were 165.154.36[.]91, 165.154.29[.]93, 165.154.11[.]140, 165.154.120[.]226, 165.154.33[.]72, and 165.154.182[.]221. Their request bodies cycled through /cgi-bin/login, /config.json, /sitemap.xml, /robots.txt, /favicon.ico, and /. Associated domains extracted via ESQL include tzrhxln[.]cn (flagged as high-entropy), leheedu[.]cn, mail.brossy[.]com[.]cn, and a malformed variant of the same. All resolve within AS-7456 and all show strong CN presence.
Practitioner takeaway: in your web proxy or honeypot logs, filter on http.request.accept-language values beginning with "zh-CN" or http.request.mime_type values containing "GBK" originating outside China 🇨🇳. Cross-reference with source AS number rather than raw IP, since VPS infrastructure rotates addresses frequently but AS attribution is stickier. The ESQL query pattern used to extract source.domain values from the filtered record set is described in the report and is straightforward to replicate against any Elastic index with HTTP header fields populated.
